personas.summary: The authoring in this package is unusually accessibility-aware: every asset carries both an alt_text and a long_description, every question carries an accessible_description, no activity is drag-only or hover-only, no option set uses positional "Structure A/B/C/D" labels, and every question type in the bank (categorize, matching, rank, route builder, curved arrow, bond-change ledger, comparison matrix, structured reasoning) is keyboard-complete through labelled Selects and IconButtons. The problem is almost entirely one of delivery and of one question type. Three barriers block publication. First, both reaction_coordinate_reasoning questions open their accessible_description with "A two-maximum energy profile", which hands over step_count — the first thing the question asks — while omitting the relative heights that the other three asks (rate-determining step, step types, overall) depend on. Second, that description never reaches the learner anyway: ReactionCoordinateQuestionRenderer looks up envelope.question.accessibilityBundle?.description while the package (and the compiled bundle) key is accessible_description, so the SVG falls back to the generic label "Schematic reaction coordinate diagram", and the minima labels sit in <text> inside an svg with role="img", where assistive technology cannot reach them — the stimulus is simply absent non-visually. Third, four structure_scaffold questions require drawing on a blank Ketcher canvas embedded as an iframe with no typed, spoken, or keyboard-composed alternative offered by the renderer. Beyond the blockers, the compiler drops content the authors wrote specifically for non-visual access: all 23 assets' long_description fields are absent from the compiled reader (molecule and reaction_coordinate blocks carry alt_text only), the synthesis roadmap compiles to an image block with an empty url so no figure exists at all, all 11 nugget practice_checks vanish, and no question-workspace renderer consumes accessible_description — questionBankApi declares the field with zero consumers. The chapter is currently available:false, so none of this is live yet.

location.anchor_text: A two-maximum energy profile is displayed with its minima labelled.

findings.observation: Both reaction_coordinate_reasoning questions (ch21-addition-elimination-profile and ch21-addition-elimination-profile-v2 share a byte-identical accessible_description) open by stating the number of maxima on the curve. The `ask` list begins with `step_count`, the answer_key gives `step_count: 2`, and the question's own level-1 hint states the equivalence outright: "Each maximum on the curve is one transition state and therefore one step." A learner reading the accessible description is handed the first sub-answer before attempting the item. The compile-time guard (find_accessibility_leaks) cannot catch this: the digit 2 is stimulus-visible in student_config.profile.step_count, and the leak is carried by the word "two-maximum", not by a flagged number or verdict token.
findings.learner_impact: A screen-reader user who does get the description (or any learner given the text equivalent) is scored on a reading-off-the-curve skill they were never asked to exercise, and the item stops measuring what it claims to measure for exactly the population the description exists to serve.
findings.evidence: topic.package.json question_sets[].accessibility_bundle.accessible_description for both profile questions: "A two-maximum energy profile is displayed with its minima labelled. Answer the questions about step count, the rate-determining step, and whether each step and the overall reaction release or absorb energy; reading those features off the curve is the task." answer_key [redacted] in both.
findings.recommended_outcome: The non-visual equivalent for a reaction-coordinate item needs to convey the curve's geometry — the sequence of rises and falls and the relative heights of each maximum and minimum against the starting level — without stating how many steps there are, which step is rate-determining, or the endergonic/exergonic classifications the item asks for.

location.anchor_text: Schematic reaction coordinate diagram

findings.observation: The reaction-coordinate stimulus is not available in any non-visual form. Three defects compound. (1) Key mismatch: [internal source reference — not in this repo], but the package, the compiled question-set, and the backend passthrough ([internal source reference — not in this repo] accessibilityBundle=resolved.accessibility_bundle) all key it as `accessible_description` — so the lookup is undefined and the SVG's aria-label falls back to the hard-coded string "Schematic reaction coordinate diagram". (2) The curve's information — minima labels "Acetyl chloride + methoxide", "Tetrahedral intermediate", "Methyl acetate + chloride", the two ‡ maxima, and the y-values that distinguish v1 from v2 — lives in <text> elements inside an <svg role="img">, whose children are not exposed to assistive technology. (3) Even the authored text would be insufficient: it says the minima are "labelled" but never states what the labels are or the relative heights, which is precisely the data rate_determining_step, step_types and overall require. That the two variants (RDS = step 1 at y=8.0 vs RDS = step 2 at y=25.0) carry identical descriptions is direct proof the text is not stimulus-specific.
findings.learner_impact: A blind or low-vision student receives a graph labelled only "Schematic reaction coordinate diagram" and four dropdowns asking about its shape. All four asks are unanswerable except by guessing. This is a required, graded activity that some learners cannot complete.
findings.evidence: [internal source reference — not in this repo] (`role="img"`, `aria-label={(envelope.question.accessibilityBundle?.description as string | undefined) ?? "Schematic reaction coordinate diagram"}`); compiled question-set.json accessibility_bundle uses key `accessible_description`; student_config.profile.control y-values 0/8.0/3.0/6.0/-20.0 (v1) vs 0/22.0/14.0/25.0/-6.0 (v2) with one shared description.
findings.recommended_outcome: Each reaction-coordinate item needs a per-variant non-visual equivalent that actually reaches the learner — the labelled species at each minimum and the relative heights of every feature must be perceivable without seeing the SVG, and whatever field carries that text must be the field the renderer reads.

location.anchor_text: The central carbon is sp³-hybridized and bears four different substituents

findings.observation: All 23 assets in the package carry an `accessibility.long_description` written specifically as the structured non-visual readout, and not one of them survives compilation. The compiled reader's molecule blocks contain only {name, smiles, alt_text, description, generator_href, rdkit_options}, and [internal source reference — not in this repo] to StructureCard; the reaction_coordinate card likewise renders `content.alt_text` twice (as the image alt and as "Described as: …") and never a long description. Grepping frontend/src for long_description/longDescription returns hits only in course-projects, orbitals and NMR code — no reader path. The dropped text is exactly the load-bearing content: the tetrahedral intermediate's four substituents and which two can be expelled, the shallow well of the rc-addition-elimination profile, why opening γ-butyrolactone yields one molecule with two groups, and that the succinic anhydride leaving group stays bonded to the chain.
findings.learner_impact: Non-visual learners get a one-sentence alt for every figure where the author wrote two to four sentences of the chemically decisive detail. Alt text like "Acetic anhydride: two acetyl groups joined through a shared oxygen atom" is adequate for identification but omits the authored consequence — that attack at either acyl carbon expels the other half as a carboxylate — which is the whole teaching point of the figure.
findings.evidence: topic.package.json assets[].accessibility.long_description present on all 23 assets; frontend/public/reader/topic-chapters/carboxylic-acid-derivatives.json contains zero occurrences of long_description; [internal source reference — not in this repo], :474, :301/:319.
findings.recommended_outcome: The authored longer descriptions need to reach the reader for every figure — a non-visual learner should be able to obtain the same level of structural detail the sighted learner reads off the drawing, not just the figure's identifying sentence.

location.anchor_text: "block_type": "image"

findings.observation: The chapter's only synthesis_roadmap asset compiles to a reader `image` block with `"url": ""` (block blk-w6qmft0f). [internal source reference — not in this repo] resolves no imageUrl and falls back to rendering content.alt_text as italic text. The result is that no figure exists for any learner, and everything the asset carried beyond the alt sentence is gone: the per-step notes ("Sulfur dioxide and hydrogen chloride leave as gases, which drives the activation to completion"; "The second equivalent of amine neutralizes the hydrogen chloride released"), the three scientific_caveats about pyridine/triethylamine substitution, direct thermal amidation, and oxalyl chloride, and the long_description. This is the same empty-image roadmap defect recorded for chapter 22.
findings.learner_impact: Sighted and non-visual learners alike lose the roadmap; the section that teaches "you cannot make an amide from an acid and an amine directly" is left with prose and two molecule cards. The alt sentence that does render names the reagents but not why they are chosen, so the reasoning the caveats carry is unavailable to everyone.
findings.evidence: frontend/public/reader/topic-chapters/carboxylic-acid-derivatives.json blk-w6qmft0f: {"url": "", "alt_text": "A two-step forward synthesis: benzoic acid is treated with thionyl chloride…", "caption": "Benzoic acid to N-methylbenzamide by way of the acid chloride"}; [internal source reference — not in this repo].
findings.recommended_outcome: The roadmap's content — the three species, the two reagent labels, why each drives the step, and the caveats about alternative acid scavengers and activating agents — needs to be delivered in the reader in some perceivable form rather than collapsing to a single alt sentence with no image behind it.

location.anchor_text: accessible_description

findings.observation: All 48 questions carry an authored accessible_description, the compiler preserves it (compiled/question-set.json accessibility_bundle.accessible_description is present on every item), and the backend passes the bundle through to the activity envelope — but no question-workspace renderer consumes it. [internal source reference — not in this repo] with zero readers anywhere in frontend/src. The only surface that renders it is [internal source reference — not in this repo], which is fed by publicQuestionDemosApi, a different data path that does not serve this chapter's bank. MolecularGeometryRenderer reads it from responseConfig (a different key path) and ReactionCoordinateQuestionRenderer reads the wrong key (see access-002). Net effect: the accessibility bundle is inert for this chapter.
findings.learner_impact: The entire non-visual scaffolding layer the authors built for this question bank is invisible in production. For question types whose stimulus is pure text (categorize, rank, multi_select) the loss is tolerable because the item text is itself readable; for anything with a rendered figure it means the learner gets whatever generic alt the renderer happens to emit and nothing else.
findings.evidence: grep of frontend/src for accessibleDescription returns only [internal source reference — not in this repo] (declaration), [internal source reference — not in this repo] (responseConfig path), and [internal source reference — not in this repo] (demo-only path); compiled/question-set.json carries accessibility_bundle on all 48 items.
findings.recommended_outcome: The authored per-question non-visual description needs an actual delivery path into the workspace a student answers in, otherwise the authoring effort and the compile-time leak guard both protect text nobody receives.

location.anchor_text: CH₃CH₂CO₂COCH₂CH₃

findings.observation: Several items make a Unicode-subscripted condensed formula the entire stimulus, and the renderers pass that string through unprocessed. [internal source reference — not in this repo] raw and sets `aria-label={`Category for ${item.text}`}`; SelectedResponseRenderer and MatchingRenderer do the same. None of the question renderers use the repo's own renderChemFormula / chemistryText normalization (which is applied in the reader and in the Newman/chair/geometry renderers but not here). Subscript code points U+2080–U+2089 are dropped or inconsistently announced by common screen readers, so "CH₃CO₂COCH₃" (i2, an anhydride) and "CH₃CO₂CH₂CH₃" (i3, an ester) can collapse to near-identical spoken strings, and "CH₃CH₂CO₂COCH₂CH₃" is a long unpunctuated run. The accessible_description does not enumerate or spell out any of the formulas — it only says six are listed.
findings.learner_impact: A screen-reader user answering ch21-classify-derivatives, its v2, ch21-name-ester and ch21-name-ester-v2 must reconstruct connectivity from an auditory stream that may not distinguish an anhydride from an ester, turning a functional-group recognition task into an audio-parsing task.
findings.evidence: student_config.items for ch21-classify-derivatives-v2: i1 CH₃CH₂CO₂CH₃, i3 CH₃CH₂CO₂COCH₂CH₃, i4 CH₃CH₂CON(CH₃)₂; prompt_text of ch21-name-ester: "Give the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH₂CO₂CH₂CH₃."; [internal source reference — not in this repo].
findings.recommended_outcome: Condensed formulas used as a sole stimulus need a spoken form that unambiguously conveys connectivity and atom counts, either through markup the screen reader handles reliably or through a per-item readout, so that family recognition rather than glyph decoding is what the item tests.

location.anchor_text: Open on acetyl chloride with the planar sp² acyl carbon highlighted

findings.observation: The three video_briefs compile to reader `video` blocks with `"url": ""` and `"is_hidden": true`; [internal source reference — not in this repo] returns null for hidden blocks, so nothing renders. Two secondary observations: the compiled block's `description` is the first storyboard direction ("Open on acetyl chloride with the planar sp² acyl carbon highlighted and the carbonyl π bond shaded"), which is production stage-direction rather than learner-facing prose and would read as nonsense if the block were ever unhidden; and the deferral notes correctly pre-record the requirements (closed captions, narration naming every visual change, a text transcript, and — for the reactivity-ladder brief — that the electron-density colour overlay must be paired with a stated pKa so the comparison is never colour-only), but nothing carries those requirements into an asset record that would be checked at production time.
findings.learner_impact: No current barrier, since the blocks do not render and the production_notes state the reader carries equivalent content in the corresponding nuggets. The risk is deferred: if these animations are produced later without the recorded caption/transcript/no-colour-only requirements travelling with them, three mechanism animations ship with no non-visual equivalent.

findings.recommended_outcome: The accessibility requirements recorded at deferral (captions, narration that names each visual change, transcript, and no colour-only encoding of the donation comparison) need to be attached to these animations in a way that survives to whenever they are actually produced, and the learner-facing description of a video block needs to be prose rather than a storyboard cue.

strengths: No activity in this chapter is drag-only, hover-only, or motion-dependent. Every question type used is keyboard-complete through labelled form controls: categorize and matching expose one labelled Select per item, rank_order uses labelled move IconButtons, synthesis_route and curved_arrow build the answer from Selects, and bond_change_ledger and comparison_matrix are real tables with per-cell aria-labels.

The bond_change_ledger items are fully answerable without seeing the structure: atom_labels are self-describing text ("1: Central tetrahedral carbon", "2: Negatively charged oxygen", "3: Chlorine", "4: Methoxy oxygen") rendered as a role="list", and the reaction_display sentence states the transformation. This is the model the other figure-bearing types should follow.

The curved_arrow items name every legal arrow endpoint in text ("Methoxide oxygen (lone pair)", "Acyl carbon of acetyl chloride"), and the site ids map correctly onto the SMILES atom indices in both variants, so arrow-drawing is achievable entirely from dropdowns.

No option set uses positional "Structure A/B/C/D" labels, and where structures are shown on single_select options they are shown on every option (ch21-recognize-lactone, ch21-ester-reduction-product, ch21-ir-identify-derivative all illustrate 4 of 4) — there is no lone-illustrated-option tell of the kind that has slipped past the leak guard in earlier chapters.

Molecule alt texts state connectivity rather than naming the image: "A tetrahedral carbon carrying a methyl group, a negatively charged oxygen, a chlorine, and a methoxy group" and "γ-Butyrolactone: a five-membered ring containing one oxygen, with the carbon adjacent to that oxygen carrying a double-bonded oxygen outside the ring" are usable readouts on their own.
The reader delivers all three detail levels (terse / standard / expanded) for every section, so a learner who needs a shorter linear pass has one without losing the section.

Aside from the two reaction_coordinate_reasoning descriptions, the accessible_descriptions are correctly task-shaped — they state the stimulus and the ask and stop ("Six condensed formulas of acyl compounds are listed, together with four family names. Assign each compound to a family; deciding which family each formula belongs to is the task.").
open_questions: Does the lti_drawing generator embed expose any non-pointer input path — a typed SMILES/name field, an atom-and-bond menu composer, or the voice structure editor referenced in [internal source reference — not in this repo] — that StructureWorkspaceRenderer simply does not advertise? I could not confirm one from the renderer or the toolbar profile; if such a path exists and is reachable from the embed, access-003 would drop from blocker to high.

Is there any surface other than the PWA reader (print/PDF export, LMS cartridge, instructor packet) that does deliver assets' long_description? If so, access-004's severity depends on which surface students are actually assigned.

Has a real screen-reader pass (NVDA/JAWS/VoiceOver) been run against the reaction_coordinate SVG and the raw Unicode-subscript question items? My findings for access-002 and access-007 are grounded in the code paths and code points, not in recorded assistive-technology output.

access-002 and access-006 are platform defects, not authoring defects — the same two would appear in any chapter using reaction_coordinate_reasoning or shipping accessibility bundles. If the orchestrator scopes this review to chapter content only, they should be routed as platform tickets rather than chapter revisions, but they still block this chapter's publication because the questions are unanswerable as delivered.

personas.summary: The chapter is figure-dense by count (21 assets, 30 figure cards in the compiled reader) but almost monotonously so by kind: 20 of the 21 assets are single static molecules, and the two non-molecule figures are the chapter's only attempt to show a relationship. One of those two — the synthesis roadmap that carries the chapter's central 'you can only run down the ladder, so activate first' idea — compiles to an image block with an empty URL and no asset_id, so a student sees italic alt text where the three-structure sequence should be. The other, the addition–elimination energy profile, renders with both end labels chopped off by the canvas edge ('etyl chloride + methoxide' on the left, 'Methyl acetate + c…' on the right). Beyond those two delivery defects, the pattern is that every idea in this chapter that is inherently a relationship — electron flow through the tetrahedral intermediate, the sp²→sp³ geometry change, the four-family reactivity ordering, amide C–N delocalization and its 20 kcal/mol rotation barrier, the carbonyl-stretch number line, the polymer repeat unit — is asserted in prose and illustrated with unannotated single structures that show none of it, with the three animations that would have carried it deferred and hidden. Meanwhile acetyl chloride and methyl acetate are each rendered five separate times with identical captions and alt text, and the spectroscopy section is four repeat structures with no spectral information at all. Legibility of the individual molecule renders is good (I rendered all 21 through the platform's own renderer): no annotation_font_scale anywhere, no oversized stereo glyphs, no label collisions — the one weak render is sodium stearate, a hairline 18-carbon chain whose carboxylate labels shrink to a few pixels at the reader's 180px card height. On the assessment side the option art is disciplined: across all 48 questions, every option/card/item list is either uniformly illustrated or uniformly text, so there is no lone-illustrated-option tell — but two lactone/lactam items give the answer away a different visual way, and six recognition and ranking items ask students to classify structures presented only as condensed formulas.

findings.observation: The chapter's only sequential/transformation figure never renders. `roadmap-acid-to-amide` is authored with three structures (benzoic acid → benzoyl chloride → N-methylbenzamide), two labelled reagent arrows and three scientific caveats, but the reader builder maps `synthesis_roadmap` to an `image` block emitted with `"url": ""` and drops the spec entirely, so none of the node SMILES reach the reader. The emitted block also carries no `asset_id`, so the reader's image-variant registry has nothing to look up even if a rendered file existed. ReaderProviderImage falls back to rendering the alt text as italic body copy, so the student sees a bordered box of prose where the roadmap should be.
findings.learner_impact: The single idea the section is built around — that an acid and an amine cannot be combined directly, so the acid must first be raised up the ladder as the chloride and then run back down — is the one thing in the chapter that most needs to be seen as a left-to-right sequence with reagents over the arrows. Every learner instead gets a paragraph of prose plus a paragraph of alt text describing a picture that is not there, and the section's other two figures (benzoyl chloride, acetyl chloride) are isolated structures that show no transformation. The compiled reader for the whole chapter therefore contains zero figures depicting a reaction.
findings.evidence: frontend/public/reader/topic-chapters/carboxylic-acid-derivatives.json, section nugget-acid-halide-reactions: image block content = {"url": "", "alt_text": "A two-step forward synthesis…", "caption": "Benzoic acid to N-methylbenzamide by way of the acid chloride"} — no asset_id, no spec. [internal source reference — not in this repo] maps synthesis_roadmap→image and line 117 emits `"url": "", # populated when a rendered file exists`. [internal source reference — not in this repo] as italic text when no image resolves. Contrast the reaction_coordinate branch ([internal source reference — not in this repo]), which inlines its spec so the reader can draw it client-side.
findings.recommended_outcome: The acid → acid chloride → amide sequence needs to arrive at the reader as something a student can see, not as a description of an absent picture; whatever carries it must show the three structures in order with the reagent for each step. Either the roadmap asset type needs the same inline-spec path the reaction-coordinate type already has, or the chapter needs a delivery route for multi-structure sequences that does not depend on a pre-rendered file.

location.anchor_text: Acetyl chloride + methoxide

findings.observation: The energy profile's two end-state labels are clipped by the canvas edge. Rendering the asset's exact spec through the same service the reader calls (`/graphs/reaction-coordinate` → reaction_coordinate_service.render_svg) produces a 760×470 viewBox in which 'Acetyl chloride + methoxide' is centred at x=64 and 'Methyl acetate + chloride' at x=732, both at font-size 13 with text-anchor="middle". At ~160 px and ~150 px of text width the first is cut by roughly 16 px on the left (it reads 'etyl chloride + methoxide') and the second by roughly 47 px on the right. The inline structure at the intermediate minimum is also small and sits close to the curve.
findings.learner_impact: The figure's whole job is to show that this is a two-step process running from named reactants, through a shallow well, to named products well below the start. With both endpoint labels mangled, the one figure that carries the energetics no longer says what the start and end states are, and a student cannot tie the shallow minimum to the tetrahedral intermediate on either side of it. It also reads as a broken page, which undermines trust in the other figures.
findings.evidence: Rendered via backend/app/services/reaction_coordinate_service.render_reaction_coordinate with the asset's spec verbatim; SVG text nodes: `<text x="64.0" y="382.9" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13">Acetyl chloride + methoxide</text>` and `<text x="732.0" … >Methyl acetate + chloride</text>` inside `viewBox="0 0 760 470"`. The rasterised output shows both labels truncated at the frame edges. Reader path: [internal source reference — not in this repo] case "reaction_coordinate" → ReactionCoordinateCard → renderReactionCoordinate(content.spec).
findings.recommended_outcome: The reactant and product identities on this profile need to be fully legible in the delivered figure — either the labels must be short enough to fit the renderer's edge minima, or the diagram needs horizontal room for labels centred on its first and last minima. Whichever route is taken, the fix should be verified against the rendered SVG rather than the spec.

location.anchor_text: Two curved arrows record this step: one runs from the lone pair of the nucleophile to the carbonyl carbon, and a second runs from the carbon–oxygen π bond to the oxygen.

findings.observation: The chapter states outright that it teaches one mechanism for its entire length, and it describes the electron flow of that mechanism in words down to the origin and destination of each arrow — but no figure anywhere in the compiled reader shows a curved arrow. The section's figures are three disconnected static structures (acetyl chloride, tetrahedral intermediate, methyl acetate) plus the energy profile; the arrows exist only in prose and in a video brief that is deferred and compiled as `is_hidden: true` with an empty URL. The same is true of the other two mechanisms the chapter narrates step by step: saponification (nugget-ester-hydrolysis, video also deferred/hidden) and amide reduction, where the prose asserts the intermediate 'expels the oxygen, not the nitrogen' with nothing showing which bond breaks.
findings.learner_impact: Electron flow is the one thing in this chapter that is genuinely spatial, and a student who wants to see where the arrow starts and ends has nowhere to look; they must hold three separate structures in mind and infer the mapping between them. Two of the chapter's own trouble spots ('drawing a one-step backside displacement at the acyl carbon' and 'omitting the tetrahedral intermediate') are precisely the errors a student makes when they have never seen the arrows drawn. The chapter then asks them to produce arrows themselves in ch21-addition-elimination-arrow and to enumerate bond and charge changes in ch21-chloride-expulsion-ledger.
findings.evidence: topic.package.json nugget-addition-elimination.text.expanded (quoted above) and nugget-ester-hydrolysis.text.expanded; asset_ids for the section are mol-acetyl-chloride, mol-tetrahedral-intermediate, mol-methyl-acetate, rc-addition-elimination — all static single species. video-addition-elimination and video-saponification carry `production_status: "deferred"`; compiled reader video blocks have `"url": ""` and `is_hidden: true`. Every one of the chapter's 21 assets is of type molecule, reaction_coordinate or synthesis_roadmap; ALLOWED_ASSET_TYPES in [internal source reference — not in this repo] contains no reaction/mechanism kind.
findings.recommended_outcome: The two-arrow addition step and the two-arrow elimination step need to be visible somewhere in the reader, with the arrow origins and destinations shown on the structures rather than named in prose. The deferral notes claim the reader already carries the same content statically; it does not, and the gap should be closed at the reader rather than deferred with the video.

location.anchor_text: acid halide > anhydride > ester > amide

findings.observation: The reactivity ladder is an ordering with two contributing quantitative axes (leaving-group basicity via conjugate-acid pKa, and π donation strength by the attached heteroatom), and the chapter's own trouble spot warns against 'treating the reactivity order as a list to memorize rather than as a consequence' of those two effects. What the reader actually delivers is four separate full-size structure cards stacked vertically — acetyl chloride, acetic anhydride, methyl acetate, acetamide — each with its own caption, none of them carrying a rank, a pKa, a donation indicator, or an arrow. The comparative video brief that would have carried the ordering is deferred and hidden.
findings.learner_impact: Nothing on the page is comparative, so the ordering has to be memorised from a sentence — exactly the failure mode the chapter names. The two effects the chapter insists reinforce one another are never shown reinforcing one another, and the directional consequence ('reactions proceed down the ladder; moving up requires returning to the acid') has no visual counterpart, which is the reasoning ch21-reactivity-rank, ch21-benzamide-synthesis-route and ch21-why-amide-least-reactive all depend on.
findings.evidence: topic.package.json nugget-reactivity-ladder.asset_ids = [mol-acetyl-chloride, mol-acetic-anhydride, mol-methyl-acetate, mol-acetamide]; compiled reader section nugget-reactivity-ladder = four independent molecule blocks plus a hidden video block. video-reactivity-ladder storyboard ('arranged left to right in order of reactivity… arrow thickness scaled to the strength of the donation… leaving-group anion below each structure with its conjugate-acid pKa') is exactly the missing comparison, and it is `production_status: "deferred"`.
findings.recommended_outcome: The four families need to be seen side by side in rank order with the two governing quantities attached to each, so the ordering is read off a comparison rather than recalled from a sentence. The permitted direction of interconversion should be visible in the same view.

findings.observation: Acetyl chloride is rendered five times in the compiled reader and methyl acetate five times, acetic anhydride and acetamide three times each — always the identical image with the identical caption and identical alt text, because the caption is the asset-level learning_goal and does not change with context. The spectroscopy section is the worst case: all four of its figure cards are repeats (the 5th, 5th, 3rd and 3rd appearance of structures the student has already scrolled past) and not one of them carries any spectroscopic information, so the section's figure strip adds nothing to the section's argument.
findings.learner_impact: Repeating an unchanged picture teaches nothing on the second through fifth showing and dilutes the signal of the figures that are new — a student scrolling the chapter learns that the pictures are decoration rather than content. In the spectroscopy section specifically, four structure cards occupy the space where the section's actual subject (band position) should be, so the student's attention is spent on structures they already know.
findings.evidence: Counted from frontend/public/reader/topic-chapters/carboxylic-acid-derivatives.json: CC(=O)Cl appears in nugget-acyl-derivative-naming, nugget-addition-elimination, nugget-reactivity-ladder, nugget-acid-halide-reactions, nugget-spectroscopy-acyl-derivatives; COC(C)=O in five sections likewise; CC(=O)OC(C)=O and CC(N)=O in three each. [internal source reference — not in this repo] sets content.description from asset.learning_goal, so the caption is byte-identical on every repeat.
findings.recommended_outcome: A structure that reappears should be doing new work at each appearance — carrying the annotation or highlight relevant to that section — or it should not reappear as a full card. The spectroscopy section in particular needs figures that carry spectral information rather than a fifth copy of structures already shown.

location.anchor_text: an amide absorbs near 1660 cm⁻¹, an ester near 1735 cm⁻¹, and an acid chloride near 1800 cm⁻¹

findings.observation: The spectroscopy concept is entirely about position on a one-dimensional wavenumber axis — five band positions in a fixed order, plus an anhydride doublet at 1820/1750 cm⁻¹ that the chapter calls 'diagnostic on its own', plus the N–H band count that separates primary, secondary and tertiary amides. None of it is drawn. There is no IR trace, no annotated wavenumber scale, and no depiction of two coupled bands, in either the reader or any of the six questions on this concept. Two of those questions (ch21-carbonyl-ir-wavenumber and its variant) ask the student to produce a numeric wavenumber, and two more (ch21-ir-identify-derivative and variant) ask them to identify a compound from band positions, without a spectrum ever having been shown.
findings.learner_impact: A number line with five marks on it is the cheapest possible visual and would replace the densest paragraph in the chapter; without it, a student has to hold five numbers, their order, and the physical reason for the order in memory simultaneously. The anhydride's two-band signature is a shape a student would recognise instantly if shown once, and asking for a numeric band position from someone who has never seen a spectrum makes the item a recall task rather than a reading task.
findings.evidence: topic.package.json nugget-spectroscopy-acyl-derivatives.asset_ids = four molecule assets, all repeats; text.expanded carries the full band list, the coupled-carbonyl explanation and the N–H band counts in prose. Compiled question set: ch21-carbonyl-ir-wavenumber (numeric, 1800 cm⁻¹ ±30), ch21-carbonyl-ir-wavenumber-v2 (1660 ±35), ch21-ir-identify-derivative and -v2 — none carries a spectrum in student_config; the option art is molecular structures only.
findings.recommended_outcome: The chapter needs the carbonyl-band ordering to be visible as positions on a shared axis, and the anhydride doublet to be seen as a doublet at least once, so band position becomes something read rather than recalled. The IR items would then be reading tasks against the same representation.

findings.observation: Hydrogen display is inconsistent inside the chapter's two four-figure comparison sets. In both nugget-reactivity-ladder and nugget-spectroscopy-acyl-derivatives the same four structures appear together, and three of them (mol-acetyl-chloride, mol-methyl-acetate, mol-acetamide) carry `rdkit_options: {show_hydrogens: true}` while mol-acetic-anhydride carries none, so it renders in plain skeletal form beside three fully-explicit neighbours. The same split runs through the chapter: 5 of 21 molecule assets set show_hydrogens, including mol-tetrahedral-intermediate (six explicit methyl hydrogens that teach nothing about the four heavy substituents that are the point) while mol-n-methylacetamide, whose classification as a *secondary* amide depends on counting one H and one methyl on nitrogen, does not.
findings.learner_impact: In a side-by-side comparison, a difference in drawing convention reads as a difference in chemistry. A student comparing four derivatives sees one drawn in a visibly different style and has to work out that the difference is cosmetic before they can make the comparison the figures exist to support, and the explicit-H clutter on the small molecules makes the acyl carbon harder to pick out at the reader's card size.
findings.evidence: topic.package.json: mol-acetyl-chloride, mol-tetrahedral-intermediate, mol-methyl-acetate, mol-acetamide, mol-methyl-thioacetate have `rdkit_options.show_hydrogens = true`; mol-acetic-anhydride, mol-n-methylacetamide, mol-methyl-propanoate and the remaining 12 have none. I rendered all 21 through backend/app/api/deck_creator.render_molecule_png with the authored options: acetamide and methyl acetate show every C–H, acetic anhydride shows none.
findings.recommended_outcome: Within any set of figures a student is meant to compare, hydrogen display needs to be uniform, and explicit hydrogens should be reserved for the figures where a hydrogen count is the teaching point (the secondary/tertiary amide distinction) rather than applied to whichever assets happened to receive the option.

findings.observation: The figure's learning_goal claims a visual separation the image does not make: 'The name of an ester is assembled from two fragments, and this structure separates them: the methyl group came from methanol and the three-carbon acyl portion from propanoic acid.' Rendered, it is an unannotated skeletal ester with no division, no colour, no bracket and no labels — nothing distinguishes the alcohol-derived fragment from the acyl fragment. The same pattern recurs: mol-2-phenylpropan-2-ol's goal says the product 'carries two identical methyl groups from the Grignard reagent and one phenyl group from the ester', but the figure marks no provenance; mol-sodium-stearate's goal turns on 'a polar head and a long nonpolar tail' with neither region marked.
findings.learner_impact: The chapter's first named trouble spot for this concept is 'naming an ester from the wrong side'. A figure that visibly split the molecule at the ester oxygen would carry that whole point; as drawn, the split exists only in the caption, so the figure adds nothing the prose has not already said and the student is left doing the parsing that the figure was supposed to remove.
findings.evidence: topic.package.json assets mol-methyl-propanoate (learning_goal quoted above, smiles CCC(=O)OC, no rdkit_options), mol-2-phenylpropan-2-ol, mol-sodium-stearate. Rendered outputs confirm no annotation layer of any kind on any of the three.
findings.recommended_outcome: Where a figure's stated purpose is to distinguish two parts of a molecule — naming fragments, reagent provenance, polar head versus nonpolar tail — that distinction needs to be visible in the image, not asserted only in the caption. Figures whose purpose cannot be made visible should have their learning_goal restated to match what they actually show.

location.anchor_text: The acyl group and the five families of carboxylic acid derivatives

findings.observation: The section that introduces the five families illustrates three of them. Its four figures are acetyl chloride (acid halide), methyl propanoate (ester), N-methylacetamide (amide) and γ-butyrolactone (a second ester) — no anhydride and no nitrile, although both are named in the title and the learning objectives and the anhydride figure already exists in the package. A student meeting the families for the first time sees esters twice and two of the five families not at all; the anhydride does not appear until three sections later, in the reactivity ladder.
findings.learner_impact: The figure strip is the visual index of the section, and here it contradicts the section's own claim of five families. The families that go unillustrated are the two the chapter's trouble spots say students misparse — the anhydride's 'two acyl carbons sharing one oxygen' pattern is exactly what a condensed formula like CH₃CO₂COCH₃ hides, and that formula is then used as a classification item in ch21-classify-derivatives.
findings.evidence: topic.package.json nugget-acyl-derivative-naming.asset_ids = [mol-acetyl-chloride, mol-methyl-propanoate, mol-n-methylacetamide, mol-butyrolactone]; learning_objectives[0] = 'Recognize an acid halide, an acid anhydride, an ester, an amide, and a nitrile as substituted acyl compounds.' mol-acetic-anhydride exists in the package but its nugget_ids are [nugget-reactivity-ladder, nugget-anhydride-reactions, nugget-spectroscopy-acyl-derivatives]. No nitrile asset exists anywhere in the chapter.
findings.recommended_outcome: At the point where the families are introduced, each family the section names needs a structure a student can see, with the anhydride pattern and the nitrile represented at least once; a second ester is not a good use of a slot while two families are unillustrated.

location.anchor_text: rotation about it is hindered by a barrier close to 20 kcal/mol

findings.observation: The amide section makes a chain of structural and energetic claims — the nitrogen lone pair delocalizes into the carbonyl, the nitrogen is planar rather than pyramidal, the C–N bond is 1.34 Å rather than 1.47 Å, rotation is hindered by ~20 kcal/mol, and the two methyls of DMF give separate NMR signals that coalesce on warming — and illustrates them with three flat single structures (acetamide, N-methylacetamide, benzamide) that show none of it. There is no resonance pair, no depiction of the planar nitrogen, and no picture of the two rotamer environments. The chapter then makes the DMF coalescence the subject of an advanced question, again with no figure.
findings.learner_impact: This is the densest stack of spatial and energetic assertions in the chapter and the one place where a static structure genuinely cannot carry the content: 'planar nitrogen' and 'restricted rotation' are shapes and motions, and a flat skeletal drawing of acetamide looks identical whether the nitrogen is planar or pyramidal. A student has to take all five claims on trust, and the DMF question then asks them to reason about two methyl environments they have never seen distinguished.
findings.evidence: topic.package.json nugget-amide-reactions.text.expanded (quoted); asset_ids = [mol-acetamide, mol-n-methylacetamide, mol-benzamide], all plain molecule renders. Question ch21-amide-hydrolysis-conditions-v2 asks why DMF's two methyl signals coalesce on warming; its student_config carries four text options and no structure. mol-n-methylacetamide's own long_description asserts 'the planar nitrogen shows the delocalization' — the render shows an ordinary 2D skeleton.
findings.recommended_outcome: The link from lone-pair delocalization to a planar nitrogen, a shortened C–N bond and a rotation barrier needs a representation in which those consequences are visible — at minimum the two contributing structures shown together, and the two methyl environments distinguished for the DMF item.

location.anchor_text: the carbon becomes sp³-hybridized in a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate

findings.observation: The geometry change at the acyl carbon is the chapter's stated reason why substitution here cannot be a backside displacement — 'the carbonyl carbon is sp²-hybridized and planar' and then 'the carbon changes from trigonal planar to tetrahedral' — but the intermediate is drawn as an ordinary flat 2D skeleton with no wedge, no dash and no 3D cue. Rendered, mol-tetrahedral-intermediate is a flat four-substituent carbon that looks geometrically no different from any other structure in the chapter, and the same flat depiction is what appears at the well of the energy profile. The video brief that would have rotated the intermediate 'so that all four substituents on the central carbon are visible' is deferred and hidden.
findings.learner_impact: The word 'tetrahedral' is doing all the work: a student who has only seen the flat drawing has no reason to believe the carbon's shape changed at all, which is precisely what makes the one-step-displacement misconception survive. The 'planar sp² carbon cannot be attacked from behind' argument is a geometric argument delivered without geometry.
findings.evidence: topic.package.json mol-tetrahedral-intermediate: smiles CC([O-])(Cl)OC, rdkit_options {show_hydrogens: true}, no stereo/wedge options; rendered output is a flat depiction with six explicit hydrogens and no 3D indication. nugget-addition-elimination.text.expanded and video-addition-elimination.storyboard[2] ('rotating it once so that all four substituents on the central carbon are visible and labelled', production_status deferred).
findings.recommended_outcome: The change in shape at the acyl carbon — planar three-substituent to tetrahedral four-substituent — needs to be visible somewhere, since it is the argument the mechanism rests on; a flat depiction of the intermediate cannot carry it.

findings.observation: Sodium stearate renders as an 18-carbon zig-zag spanning nearly the full width of a 440×340 canvas, so the structure collapses into a thin horizontal hairline occupying about a fifth of the frame's height, with the carboxylate O and O⁻ labels drawn at a small fraction of the canvas. The reader constrains the image to maxH 180px, scaling the whole render to roughly 233px wide, at which point the charge label is a few pixels tall. The disconnected Na⁺ floats unattached in the middle of the empty upper area, visually unrelated to the anion. Nothing marks the polar head or the nonpolar tail.
findings.learner_impact: The figure exists to make one point — a charged head on a long greasy tail — and at delivered size that point is carried by a hairline whose charged end is the least legible thing in the frame. A student cannot read the charge that makes it a soap, and the free-floating sodium ion invites the reading that it is a separate species in the drawing rather than the counter-ion.
findings.evidence: topic.package.json mol-sodium-stearate: smiles CCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCC(=O)[O-].[Na+], no rdkit_options; learning_goal cites 'a polar head and a long nonpolar tail'. Rendered through render_molecule_png at the platform default (440,340); [internal source reference — not in this repo] sets the reader image to maxH="180px".
findings.recommended_outcome: The amphiphile figure needs its charged head legible at reader size and its two regions distinguishable — either by a depiction that does not force an 18-carbon chain across the full frame, or by marking the head and tail regions explicitly.

location.anchor_text: Both ends remain reactive, so condensation continues, and the result is a polyamide.

findings.observation: The polymer section illustrates four monomers (adipic acid, hexane-1,6-diamine, terephthalic acid, caprolactam) and never draws a polymer. There is no repeat unit, no chain fragment showing the amide or ester linkages that join the units, and no depiction of the step-growth-versus-chain-growth contrast that the section spends two paragraphs on — a contrast about how monomer concentration and chain length change over the course of the reaction, which is a graph-shaped idea delivered as prose.
findings.learner_impact: A student can end the section able to name the monomers but never having seen what a polyamide chain looks like or where the new bond sits, which is the thing the section is about. The step-versus-chain distinction is assessed twice (ch21-monomer-pairs-categorize and ch21-polyamide-monomers) on the basis of statements about monomer disappearance and molecular-weight growth that were never shown.
findings.evidence: topic.package.json nugget-step-growth-polymers.asset_ids = [mol-adipic-acid, mol-hexane-1-6-diamine, mol-terephthalic-acid, mol-caprolactam] — four isolated monomers; text.expanded contains the full kinetic contrast ('monomer disappears early while high molecular weight is reached only at very high conversion' versus 'full-length chains coexist with unreacted monomer throughout'). Compiled reader section nugget-step-growth-polymers = four molecule blocks and one external link.
findings.recommended_outcome: The section needs the linkage that joins two monomers, and the repeat unit that results, to be visible at least once; the step-growth versus chain-growth contrast needs a representation in which the difference in how chains build up can be seen rather than only read.

findings.observation: Six items ask students to recognise or rank compounds by structural class while presenting those compounds only as condensed formulas, with no structures — even though the chapter already owns renderable structures for most of them. ch21-classify-derivatives and its variant list items such as 'CH₃CO₂COCH₃' and 'CH₃CH₂CO₂COCH₂CH₃' with 0 of 6 items illustrated; ch21-reactivity-rank and its variant present 0 of 4 cards illustrated; ch21-name-ester and its variant give 'CH₃CH₂CH₂CO₂CH₂CH₃' and 'CH₃CO₂CH(CH₃)₂' as the entire stimulus. The chapter's own preferred_representations for this concept is 'molecule'.
findings.learner_impact: The intended task is classification and ranking; parsing a condensed formula is a second, unrelated task layered on top, and it is the task the chapter's trouble spots say students fail ('naming an ester from the wrong side', 'confusing a secondary amide with an amine'). A student who cannot see that CH₃CO₂COCH₃ contains two acyl carbons sharing an oxygen is being assessed on notation decoding rather than on whether they know what an anhydride is.
findings.evidence: Compiled question-set.json: ch21-classify-derivatives items 0/6 with structure_smiles, ch21-classify-derivatives-v2 0/6, ch21-reactivity-rank cards 0/4, ch21-reactivity-rank-v2 0/4, ch21-name-ester and -v2 short_answer with a condensed formula in prompt_text only. topic.package.json concepts[0].preferred_representations = ["molecule"]; the platform enriches any entry carrying structure_smiles into a rendered image ([internal source reference — not in this repo]), which these items do not supply.
findings.recommended_outcome: Where the task is to recognise or rank a structural class, the student needs to see the structure, not decode a condensed string; the notation-parsing load should be separated from the classification being assessed.

findings.observation: In ch21-recognize-lactone the stem describes the target compound verbally ('a five-membered ring containing one oxygen, with a double-bonded oxygen on the ring carbon adjacent to it') and then attaches a *different* structure to each of the four options: option a is O=C1CCCO1 (exactly the described ring), b is cyclopentanone, c is tetrahydrofuran, d is succinic anhydride. Only one option's picture matches the stem's description, so the key can be selected by matching the drawn ring to the words without evaluating any of the four claims. ch21-recognize-lactone-v2 is built identically for caprolactam (option a = O=C1CCCCCN1, the only structure matching the described seven-membered N-containing ring).
findings.learner_impact: The item is meant to test whether a student knows that a cyclic ester is still an ester and what that implies for hydrolysis; as built, a student who can read a ring drawing gets it right without engaging the classification at all, and a student who reasons correctly but distrusts the picture-matching shortcut gets no benefit. The option art, which is otherwise a strength of this bank, here does the answering.
findings.evidence: topic.package.json question_sets ch21-recognize-lactone: prompt_text describes the compound; options a–d each carry a distinct structure_smiles (O=C1CCCO1 / O=C1CCCC1 / C1CCOC1 / O=C1CCC(=O)O1) and only a matches the stem. ch21-recognize-lactone-v2: options O=C1CCCCCN1 / C1CCCNCC1 / O=C1CCCCCO1 / C1CCCC=NCC1, only a matches. Both compiled with 4/4 options illustrated.
findings.recommended_outcome: These two items need the compound under discussion to be fixed once — shown in the stem or named — so the options differ in their claims rather than in which structure they depict; as built, the illustration set identifies the key independently of the chemistry.

findings.observation: The bond-change ledger's atom numbering is delivered as a text legend beside an unnumbered picture, and one legend entry names the wrong atom. The renderer draws molecule_smiles through plain RDKit with no atom indices and lists the labels separately as '1: Central tetrahedral carbon … 5: Methyl carbon attached to the central carbon'. For CC([O-])(Cl)OC the RDKit indices are 0=acetyl methyl, 1=central C, 2=O⁻, 3=Cl, 4=methoxy O, 5=methoxy methyl — and the answer key's rows ('1-3', '1-2', charge on '2' and '3') confirm the ids are RDKit indices. Id 5 therefore points at the methyl on the methoxy oxygen, not at 'the methyl carbon attached to the central carbon'. The same label appears in the -v2 item on CC([O-])(N)OC with the same offset.
findings.learner_impact: A student must map legend numbers onto a drawing that carries no numbers; for the uniquely identifiable atoms (the chlorine, the charged oxygen) that is workable, but a student who follows the legend to locate the methyl on the central carbon is sent to the wrong atom, and any row they enter using number 5 describes a bond that is not there. It also quietly teaches a wrong reading of the structure at the exact moment the student is being asked to reason about which bond breaks.
findings.evidence: topic.package.json ch21-chloride-expulsion-ledger.student_config.atom_labels id '5' = 'Methyl carbon attached to the central carbon'; answer_key.expected_rows use atoms '1-3', '1-2', '2', '3'. [internal source reference — not in this repo] renders with rdMolDraw2D and no addAtomIndices; [internal source reference — not in this repo] shows the SVG and then the id:text legend as separate elements.
findings.recommended_outcome: The atom numbers the answer depends on need to be visible on the structure the student is looking at, and every legend entry must name the atom its number actually resolves to.

findings.observation: Every one of the 21 assets carries a carefully written `accessibility.long_description` and none of them reaches the reader. The reader builder sets each figure block's `description` from the asset's `learning_goal` and emits only `alt_text` alongside it, so the longer structured description — which is where the figures' spatial content actually lives ('the ring holds four carbons and one oxygen…', 'two of these, the chlorine and the methoxy group, could be expelled…') — is dropped at compile time for the whole chapter, including for the reaction-coordinate profile and the roadmap.
findings.learner_impact: This falls hardest on the figures whose visual content is thin or absent: for the roadmap, whose image never renders, the long_description is the only thing that could have described the three-structure sequence, and it is discarded in favour of the one-line alt text. More generally, the reader's figure captions are all purpose statements, so a student who wants to know what they are looking at, rather than why, has nowhere to read it. (Overlaps the Accessibility persona — flagging per rubric.)
findings.evidence: [internal source reference — not in this repo] lines 78-104: `alt` comes from accessibility.alt_text and `description` from asset.learning_goal; `long_description` is never read. Confirmed in the compiled reader: mol-acetyl-chloride's block description is its learning_goal verbatim, and no block in the file contains any long_description text.
findings.recommended_outcome: The authored per-figure descriptions need a delivery path to the reader, or the chapter should stop authoring content into a field the pipeline discards; this matters most for figures whose image is missing or whose spatial content is not otherwise shown.

findings.observation: Several transformation questions carry no structural stimulus even though the chapter owns the relevant structures. ch21-anhydride-acetylation asks what becomes of acetic anhydride when it acetylates salicylic acid, with four text-only options and no structure, though mol-aspirin, mol-acetic-anhydride and mol-succinic-anhydride all exist; its variant does the same for succinic anhydride ring-opening. ch21-polyamide-monomers and ch21-monomer-pairs-categorize match and sort monomers with 0 of 4 and 0 of 6 entries illustrated, though all four monomer structures exist in the package. The four structure_scaffold items ('Hydroxide adds to methyl acetate. Draw the tetrahedral intermediate…') present a blank canvas with the substrate named only in words.
findings.learner_impact: Each of these asks the student to track atoms through a transformation — which half of the anhydride leaves, whether the expelled carboxylate is still tethered, which end of a monomer condenses — while giving them nothing to track the atoms on. For the draw-the-intermediate items in particular, the student must first reconstruct the substrate from its name before they can transform it, which adds recall load to a task meant to test the transformation.
findings.evidence: Compiled question-set.json: ch21-anhydride-acetylation and -v2 options 0/4 with structure_smiles; ch21-polyamide-monomers left 0/4 right 0/4; ch21-monomer-pairs-categorize items 0/6; ch21-tetrahedral-intermediate-draw, -v2, ch21-amide-reduction-draw and -v2 have student_config [redacted] with no molecule_smiles. By contrast ch21-grignard-ester-error and both curved_arrow items do supply molecule_smiles, showing the stimulus route is available.
findings.recommended_outcome: Questions that ask a student to follow atoms through a transformation need the starting structure visible; the substrate should not have to be reconstructed from its name before the assessed reasoning can begin.

strengths: No figure in the chapter carries the known annotation_font_scale defect — only 5 of 21 assets set any rdkit_options at all, and those set show_hydrogens alone, so there are no oversized stereo glyphs anywhere.

I rendered all 21 assets through the platform's own renderer (backend/app/api/deck_creator.render_molecule_png) with their authored options: every structure is chemically legible, with no labels sitting on bonds, no atom-label collisions, and no molecule too dense to parse. Aspirin, succinic anhydride, caprolactam and acetyl phosphate in particular read cleanly at card size.

Across all 48 compiled questions there is no lone-illustrated-option tell: every options/cards/items/left/right/cases list is either uniformly illustrated (4/4, 5/5, 2/2) or uniformly text-only. Option art is supplied consistently for single_select product choices, matching_pairs right-hand columns, comparison_matrix cases and synthesis_route intermediates.

Every asset referenced by a nugget reaches the compiled reader — 21 assets producing 30 figure blocks with no dangling asset_ids and no silently dropped figures (only the roadmap's image bytes are missing, not the block).
The three deferred videos compile as is_hidden with empty URLs, so the reader shows no dead 'Watch' links or broken players — the deferral is handled cleanly even though it leaves content gaps.

The reaction-coordinate asset inlines its full spec so the reader draws it client-side with structures at each minimum, including the tetrahedral intermediate at the shallow well — the one figure in the chapter that genuinely shows a relationship rather than a species.
Alt text is written per figure and is specific and structural throughout (e.g. mol-succinic-anhydride, rc-addition-elimination), not generic restatements of the title.
open_questions: Is a rendered file for synthesis_roadmap assets ever produced in this pipeline? The compiled image block carries neither a URL nor an asset_id, so ReaderProviderImage cannot resolve a variant from the registry even if one were published — I could not find a path by which this figure ever becomes an image.

Are bond_change_ledger atom_labels ids intended to be RDKit atom indices? The answer keys are consistent with that reading, which is what makes id '5' a mislabel; if the ids are meant as free display keys, visual-016's mislabel claim weakens to a legend-wording issue but the 'numbers not shown on the figure' half still stands.

Is the reaction-coordinate label clipping expected to be fixed at the renderer (padding for edge minima) or at the authoring layer (shorter minima_labels)? Other chapters using two-species minima labels are likely to hit the same 760px edge, so this may be a platform-wide figure defect rather than a ch21 authoring choice.

The topic-package schema's ALLOWED_ASSET_TYPES has no reaction/mechanism kind, while the reader block renderer already supports a `reaction` block with reaction_smiles. Is that surface reachable from a topic package by any route? Several of my visual-opportunity findings would collapse into one intervention if it is.

personas.summary: NOT-GO as it stands, but the gap to publishable is small. I independently parsed and canonicalized all 21 asset SMILES, the 3 roadmap nodes, the 3 reaction-coordinate minima, and every structure_smiles/molecule_smiles/answer_key SMILES in all 48 question sets with RDKit: every one is valid, every molecular formula matches its stated identity, and every product/reactant claim I checked is mass- and charge-balanced (acetic anhydride C4H6O3 matches the C4H6O3 in the IR question; propanamide and DMF are correctly both C3H7NO so the N-H band count is genuinely load-bearing; sodium stearate is C18; the acid-chloride product ladder ethanol/acetone/tert-butanol/ethyl acetate is correct for LiAlH4 / Me2CuLi / excess MeMgBr / EtOH-pyridine). All 24 surfaced answer keys are chemically correct, the two reaction-coordinate profiles' rate-determining-step keys are correctly read off their own control points (step 1 for the 8-vs-6 profile, step 2 for the 22-vs-25 profile), the curved-arrow site indices map exactly onto the SMILES atom order, and the compiled question-set is byte-identical to the package. The reactivity ladder, saponification stoichiometry, DMF rotational barrier, thioester orbital argument, and the entire IR section are accurate. Two things block publication. First, one genuinely wrong chemistry claim: nugget-acid-halide-reactions tells students a Grignard reagent adds a second time because the ketone is 'more reactive' than the acid chloride, which inverts the chapter's own reactivity ladder. Second, both lactone/lactam recognition items render a different compound under each option, so the correct option is the only one whose picture matches the compound named in the prompt and can be chosen with no chemistry at all. Beyond those, the chapter over-generalizes two heuristics ('the weaker base is expelled', 'interconversions never run up the ladder') that its own later sections and its own distractor reagent list contradict, ships no worked example and no curved-arrow mechanism figure for its central mechanism, and delivers a broken empty image where the synthesis roadmap should be. Fix the two blockers and qualify the two heuristics and I would assign this chapter.

location.anchor_text: first substituting to give a ketone and then adding to that more reactive ketone

findings.observation: The standard-depth text states that a Grignard reagent adds twice to an acid chloride 'first substituting to give a ketone and then adding to that more reactive ketone'. A ketone is not more reactive than an acid chloride toward a carbon nucleophile; the acid halide sits at the top of the reactivity ladder that this same chapter establishes two sections earlier (acid halide > anhydride > ester > amide). The expanded text repeats the error in a self-referential form: 'a ketone is more electrophilic than the acid chloride's substitution product would suggest' — the acid chloride's substitution product IS that ketone, so the sentence compares the ketone with itself and supplies no reason at all. The correct explanation for double addition from an acid chloride is kinetic and stoichiometric (the ketone formed in situ is still highly electrophilic and there is unconsumed Grignard reagent present), not a reversal of the reactivity order. Note that the analogous statement for esters, in nugget-ester-other-reactions and in the ch21-grignard-ester-error repair option, is correct and correctly justified ('it lacks the electron-donating alkoxy group'); the error is the illegitimate transfer of that ester argument to acid chlorides, where chlorine is not a net π donor strong enough to make the acyl carbon less electrophilic than a ketone's.
findings.learner_impact: A student reading the acid-halide section builds a reactivity order in which ketones outrank acid chlorides, directly contradicting the ladder they are asked to reproduce in ch21-reactivity-rank and to reason from in ch21-why-amide-least-reactive. On an exam they will predict that an acid chloride is attacked more slowly than the ketone it produces, and will mis-explain why a cuprate stops at the ketone.
findings.evidence: nugget-acid-halide-reactions text.standard: '...A Grignard reagent adds twice, first substituting to give a ketone and then adding to that more reactive ketone, so the isolated product is a tertiary alcohol.' text.expanded: 'The first addition of a Grignard reagent produces a ketone, but a ketone is more electrophilic than the acid chloride's substitution product would suggest and is attacked immediately by a second equivalent of the reagent...'. Compare nugget-reactivity-ladder text.standard: 'giving acid halide > anhydride > ester > amide'. Both depth variants are shipped to the reader (frontend/public/reader/topic-chapters/carboxylic-acid-derivatives.json carries all three in _detail_texts).
findings.recommended_outcome: The acid-halide section needs a correct, non-circular reason for the second Grignard addition — one that does not claim the ketone outranks the acid chloride, and that keeps the (correct) ester-case argument distinct from the acid-halide case. Both the standard and expanded depth texts must be corrected together.

location.anchor_text: Which statement about this compound is correct?

findings.observation: Both recognition items attach a different molecule to each option, and only the correct option's molecule is the compound named in the prompt. In ch21-recognize-lactone the prompt describes 'a five-membered ring containing one oxygen, with a double-bonded oxygen on the ring carbon adjacent to it'; option a carries O=C1CCCO1 (that exact compound), while b carries cyclopentanone, c carries tetrahydrofuran, and d carries succinic anhydride. In ch21-recognize-lactone-v2 the prompt describes caprolactam; option a carries O=C1CCCCCN1 (that exact compound), while b carries azepane, c carries a seven-membered lactone, and d carries an eight-membered cyclic imine. A student who can read a structure but knows nothing about ester/ketone/ether/anhydride or amide/amine/ester/imine classification selects the correct option by matching the picture to the prompt's word description. The distractor figures are also false as figures: each is captioned by a claim about 'this compound' while depicting a different compound.
findings.learner_impact: The item measures structure-reading, not the classification skill it is written to assess, and it will report mastery of the naming/recognition concept that a student does not have. Two of the three surfaced questions for the naming concept are affected (this item and its variant), so the concept's assessment signal is largely spurious.
findings.evidence: ch21-recognize-lactone.student_config.options[*].structure_smiles = O=C1CCCO1 / O=C1CCCC1 / C1CCOC1 / O=C1CCC(=O)O1 (RDKit formulas C4H6O2, C5H8O, C4H8O, C4H4O3 — four distinct compounds). ch21-recognize-lactone-v2 options = O=C1CCCCCN1 / C1CCCNCC1 / O=C1CCCCCO1 / C1CCCC=NCC1 (C6H11NO, C6H13N, C6H10O2, C7H13N). Prompt text names the compound and describes its ring size and heteroatoms explicitly.
findings.recommended_outcome: These two items need an option set in which the structure cannot discriminate — either every option shows the same subject compound (or no option shows a structure) and only the classification claim varies. The eight-membered imine distractor in the variant also needs to match the subject's ring size so ring-atom counting is not a second tell.

findings.observation: The synthesis_roadmap asset compiles into the reader as an image block with an empty url and is_hidden absent (i.e. visible): {"url": "", "alt_text": "A two-step forward synthesis...", "caption": "Benzoic acid to N-methylbenzamide by way of the acid chloride"}. The three deferred video briefs were correctly compiled with is_hidden: true; the roadmap was not. It is the only non-molecule figure in the acid-halide section and the only figure anywhere in the chapter that shows a multi-step transformation with reagents on the arrows.
findings.learner_impact: Students see a captioned empty frame in the section that most needs a sequence figure, and the roadmap's teaching content (why the acid must be activated before the amine is introduced, and why two equivalents of methylamine are used) reaches them only as prose. The paired question ch21-benzamide-synthesis-route asks them to reconstruct exactly this route with no worked visual to have studied.
findings.evidence: frontend/public/reader/topic-chapters/carboxylic-acid-derivatives.json, section nugget-acid-halide-reactions, block_type 'image', content.url == "" and no is_hidden flag, whereas the three video blocks in sections nugget-addition-elimination / nugget-reactivity-ladder / nugget-ester-hydrolysis carry is_hidden: true.
findings.recommended_outcome: The acid-halide section needs its acid-to-amide route to actually render, or the block needs to be suppressed the way deferred videos are so students are not shown a broken figure. Either way the roadmap's reagent/rationale content must reach the reader in some rendered form.

findings.observation: The chapter's stated organizing idea is that one mechanism explains everything in it, and the expanded text describes the arrow bookkeeping in words in detail ('one runs from the lone pair of the nucleophile to the carbonyl carbon, and a second runs from the carbon–oxygen π bond to the oxygen ... one from an oxygen lone pair back into the carbon–oxygen bond and one from the bond to the departing group'). No figure in the chapter shows a single curved arrow. The section's assets are three static molecule renders (acetyl chloride, the tetrahedral intermediate, methyl acetate) plus an energy profile; the one asset that would have animated the electron flow, video-addition-elimination, is production_status 'deferred' and compiles hidden.
findings.learner_impact: The electron-flow bookkeeping that ch21-addition-elimination-arrow and ch21-chloride-expulsion-ledger both grade is taught only in prose, so students must translate a paragraph of arrow prose into a drawn mechanism with no worked visual model. This is the single highest-leverage figure gap in the chapter.
findings.evidence: nugget-addition-elimination.asset_ids = [mol-acetyl-chloride, mol-tetrahedral-intermediate, mol-methyl-acetate, rc-addition-elimination]; video_briefs[0].production_status = 'deferred'; compiled reader section nugget-addition-elimination contains three molecule blocks, one reaction_coordinate block, and one hidden video block.
findings.recommended_outcome: The addition–elimination section needs a static, arrow-annotated depiction of both steps (source and destination of each electron pair, and the sp²→sp³→sp² geometry change) that does not depend on the deferred video pipeline.

location.anchor_text: When the tetrahedral intermediate carries two potential leaving groups, the weaker base is expelled. That single principle sets both the direction of every interconversion in this chapter

findings.observation: Nugget 2 states the expulsion rule as universal and calls it 'that single principle', and the concept's third learning objective is to 'Predict which group is expelled from a tetrahedral intermediate carrying two potential leaving groups'. Nugget 6 then presents the chapter's most important ester reaction as a case where the rule gives the wrong answer: in saponification the intermediate expels alkoxide, 'which is the more basic of the two available leaving groups'. Nugget 6 explains the local reason (expelling hydroxide merely returns starting material, and the subsequent proton transfer removes the product) but never flags that it has just overridden the principle stated in nugget 2, and nugget 2 is never amended.
findings.learner_impact: A student who has internalized 'the weaker base leaves' and applies it to hydroxide + ester predicts that hydroxide is re-expelled and that saponification does not occur. The rule is the chapter's central predictive tool, so an unmarked exception in its most-assessed application is a durable source of wrong predictions.
findings.evidence: nugget-addition-elimination text.standard: 'When the tetrahedral intermediate carries two potential leaving groups, the weaker base is expelled. That single principle sets both the direction of every interconversion in this chapter and the reactivity order of the derivatives.' nugget-ester-hydrolysis text.standard: 'The tetrahedral intermediate expels alkoxide, which is the more basic of the two available leaving groups but is nevertheless lost because the alternative is expelling hydroxide and returning to starting material.'
findings.recommended_outcome: The mechanism section needs the expulsion heuristic stated with its scope — it decides between two chemically different groups, and it is superseded when the alternative simply regenerates the starting material or when an irreversible downstream proton transfer supplies the driving force. The saponification section should explicitly cross-reference that qualification.

location.anchor_text: Interconversions run down the reactivity ladder, never up

findings.observation: The ladder is built from four families only; the carboxylic acid is never placed on it, yet the chapter repeatedly speaks of 'hydrolysis back to the carboxylic acid' as the way to move 'up'. The rule is then stated without exception in ch21-benzamide-synthesis-route's feedback ('Interconversions run down the reactivity ladder, never up'), while that same question's reagent list offers 'CH₃OH, H₂SO₄ (cat.)' — Fischer esterification, which converts benzoic acid directly to methyl benzoate and which nugget-ester-hydrolysis explicitly teaches ('the reverse of this sequence is Fischer esterification'). Amide hydrolysis to the carboxylic acid is likewise not classifiable as up or down on a ladder that has no rung for the acid.
findings.learner_impact: A student who knows Fischer esterification sees the chapter's absolute rule falsified by a reagent printed in the same question, and a student who does not know it takes away a rule that will forbid a transformation they are expected to perform. Neither can locate the carboxylic acid when asked to plan a route, which is the actual skill the synthesis_route items test.
findings.evidence: nugget-reactivity-ladder text.expanded: 'Reactions proceed down the ladder ... Moving up the ladder requires hydrolysis back to the carboxylic acid followed by treatment with a reagent such as thionyl chloride.' ch21-benzamide-synthesis-route.feedback_bundle.generic_incorrect_explanation: 'Interconversions run down the reactivity ladder, never up...' with student_config.reagents including r_meoh 'CH₃OH, H₂SO₄ (cat.)'. nugget-ester-hydrolysis text.expanded: 'Since the reverse of this sequence is Fischer esterification, the position of the equilibrium is controlled by concentration...'.
findings.recommended_outcome: The reactivity section needs the carboxylic acid placed explicitly on the ladder and the directional rule qualified so that acid-catalysed, equilibrium-driven conversions (Fischer esterification, transesterification) are visibly compatible with it rather than apparent counterexamples.

location.anchor_text: A backside displacement is geometrically impossible here

findings.observation: The chapter asserts that concerted backside displacement at an acyl carbon is 'geometrically impossible' and that every reaction in the chapter proceeds through a discrete tetrahedral intermediate. Both are stronger than the evidence supports: for the most reactive substrates (acyl halides with weakly basic nucleophiles) the tetrahedral species is often not a minimum on the potential-energy surface at all and the substitution is concerted, and in-plane concerted acyl substitution is a recognized mechanistic class. The correct teaching claim is energetic and structural — addition is accessible because the π* orbital offers a low-energy destination for the electron pair, so the addition–elimination path dominates — not that the alternative is geometrically forbidden.
findings.learner_impact: Students are given an absolute they will have to un-learn, and the useful reasoning (compare the energetic cost of the two pathways) is replaced by an assertion they cannot check. It also makes the chapter's own energy profile look decorative: if the alternative were geometrically impossible there would be nothing for the profile to argue about.
findings.evidence: nugget-addition-elimination text.standard: 'A backside displacement is geometrically impossible here: the carbonyl carbon is sp²-hybridized and planar, and the π system provides a low-energy destination for the electron pair, making addition the accessible pathway.' The learning_goal of rc-addition-elimination states the intended claim correctly: 'passes through a discrete tetrahedral intermediate sitting in a shallow well, rather than through a single concerted step.'
findings.recommended_outcome: The mechanism section needs 'geometrically impossible' replaced by an energetic comparison, with an acknowledgement that the tetrahedral species is a shallow minimum whose existence is substrate-dependent.

location.anchor_text: Draw the single curved arrow for the first step of the mechanism.

findings.observation: Both curved_arrow items set max_arrows: 1 and ask for 'the single curved arrow for the first step', while the section they assess teaches that the addition step takes two arrows — 'Two curved arrows record this step: one runs from the lone pair of the nucleophile to the carbonyl carbon, and a second runs from the carbon–oxygen π bond to the oxygen.' The items' own level-3 hints restate the two-arrow picture ('The carbonyl carbon accepts the electron pair, and the π electrons move onto oxygen as it does'), so the question tells students the second arrow exists and then makes it impossible to draw. The expected arrow itself (lone pair on site 0 → atom site 3 / site 2) is correct, and I verified the site ids map exactly onto the RDKit atom order of both molecule_smiles strings.
findings.learner_impact: A student who has learned the chapter's arrow convention correctly cannot enter the step they were taught, and receives credit for a half-step. The habit of omitting the π-bond arrow is precisely the bookkeeping error that produces pentavalent carbons later in the mechanism.
