findings.evidence: ch21-addition-elimination-arrow.student_config.max_arrows = 1 with expected_arrows of length 1; nugget-addition-elimination text.expanded: 'Two curved arrows record this step...'; the same question's hints[2]. Identical pattern in ch21-addition-elimination-arrow-v2.
findings.recommended_outcome: The mechanism items need to accept the full two-arrow addition step that the chapter teaches, or the prompt and hints need to state explicitly which one of the two arrows is being asked for and why the other is omitted.

location.anchor_text: Methyl carbon attached to the central carbon

findings.observation: The atom_labels use zero-based SMILES atom indices — labels 1, 2, 3 and 4 correctly name the central carbon, the O⁻, the leaving atom and the methoxy oxygen for CC([O-])(Cl)OC — but label id '5' is given as 'Methyl carbon attached to the central carbon'. Atom 5 is the methyl carbon of the methoxy group; the methyl attached to the central carbon is atom 0 and carries no label. Both ledger items have the identical mislabel (ch21-chloride-expulsion-ledger and -v2 on CC([O-])(N)OC). The expected_rows themselves are chemically correct and do not reference atom 5 or atom 0, so grading is unaffected.
findings.learner_impact: The molecule contains two methyl groups and the only labelled one is labelled as the other. A student working out which bond breaks must disambiguate the two oxygens and the two methyls from a label set that misdirects them, which turns a mechanism-bookkeeping item into a puzzle about the labelling scheme.
findings.evidence: RDKit atom order for CC([O-])(Cl)OC: 0 C (methyl on central C), 1 C (central), 2 O⁻, 3 Cl, 4 O (methoxy), 5 C (methyl on methoxy O). student_config.atom_labels = [{'1','Central tetrahedral carbon'},{'2','Negatively charged oxygen'},{'3','Chlorine'},{'4','Methoxy oxygen'},{'5','Methyl carbon attached to the central carbon'}]. Same in -v2 for CC([O-])(N)OC.
findings.recommended_outcome: The two ledger items need their fifth atom label corrected to name the atom it actually points at, and ideally both methyl carbons labelled so the two oxygens and two methyls are unambiguous.

findings.observation: Three of the six questions tagged to concept 3 (relative-reactivity-of-acyl-derivatives, order 3) require content introduced much later in the chapter. ch21-reactivity-rank-v2 asks students to place S-methyl thiobenzoate in the ladder, an idea taught only in nugget-biological-acyl-transfer (concept order 8). ch21-why-amide-least-reactive offers, as one of three pieces of expected evidence, the amide-versus-acid-chloride carbonyl IR positions, taught only in nugget-spectroscopy-acyl-derivatives (concept order 10); nugget-reactivity-ladder itself never mentions an infrared frequency. ch21-ester-vs-amide-matrix-v2 has an 'two carbonyl absorptions' row from the same later section.
findings.learner_impact: A student practising section 3 as they read hits items that cannot be answered from anything they have read, which reads as a knowledge gap rather than a sequencing artefact. Instructors assigning the chapter section by section will get spurious failure rates on the reactivity concept.
findings.evidence: ch21-reactivity-rank-v2.concept_slug = 'relative-reactivity-of-acyl-derivatives' with card 'S-Methyl thiobenzoate, C₆H₅COSCH₃'; the thioester argument appears only in nugget-biological-acyl-transfer (order 9, concept order 8). ch21-why-amide-least-reactive.answer_key.fields.evidence.expected_option_ids includes 'ir' ('carbonyl stretching absorption of an amide lies near 1660 cm⁻¹ ... acid chloride near 1800 cm⁻¹'); nugget-reactivity-ladder contains no wavenumbers.
findings.recommended_outcome: Either these three items need to be re-tagged to the later concepts whose content they require, or the reactivity section needs a forward-looking sentence that supplies the thioester rung and the IR correlation at the point the ladder is introduced.

findings.observation: Three variant pairs are labelled variant_of but assess materially different objectives, and the compiled bank surfaces 24 items with 24 staged variants — so a cohort served the variant is never assessed on the base item's objective. ch21-amide-hydrolysis-conditions (products and conditions of forcing amide hydrolysis) is paired with -v2 (why the DMF methyl signals coalesce on warming). ch21-ester-reduction-product (LiAlH4 reduction stopping point) is paired with -v2 (transesterification regiochemistry) — the slug still says 'reduction'. ch21-grignard-ester-error (double Grignard addition) is paired with -v2 (saponification stoichiometry). Contrast the well-formed pairs, e.g. ch21-recognize-lactone / -v2 (lactone then lactam) and ch21-tetrahedral-intermediate-draw / -v2, which swap the substrate and hold the objective fixed.
findings.learner_impact: Two students taking the same assignment are tested on different learning objectives, and the item bank's per-objective coverage claims are not reliable. Amide hydrolysis conditions and ester reduction — both core, both named in learning_objectives — can be missed entirely depending on which variant is served.
findings.evidence: ch21-amide-hydrolysis-conditions.prompt_text 'Benzamide is heated for several hours with concentrated aqueous sodium hydroxide...' vs ch21-amide-hydrolysis-conditions-v2.prompt_text 'The two methyl groups of N,N-dimethylformamide give two separate signals in its proton NMR spectrum...', variant_of: 'ch21-amide-hydrolysis-conditions'. compiled/question-set.json counts: {'surfaced': 24, 'staged_variants': 24}.
findings.recommended_outcome: Variant pairs need to hold the assessed objective constant; the three mismatched items should become standalone questions on their own objectives so that neither objective can be dropped by a variant swap.

location.anchor_text: practice_check

findings.observation: All eleven nuggets carry a practice_check with a prompt and a model answer, and I verified all eleven answers are chemically correct (methyl propanoate; chloride expulsion; the two-effect amide argument; the 50% methylamine yield; ethyl acetate plus acetic acid; the stoichiometric hydroxide; 2-phenylpropan-2-ol; N,N-dimethylethylamine; the thioester orbital argument; the polyester/polyamide pairing; acetic anhydride from C4H6O3 with two bands). None of them reaches the reader: the compiled chapter contains only text, molecule, reaction_coordinate, image, video, mcmurry_link and external_link blocks.
findings.learner_impact: Eleven authored retrieval opportunities — one per section, sized for immediate self-check while reading — are written and then discarded, leaving the reader as continuous prose with no in-section checkpoint. The only practice a student can reach is the question bank, which is a separate surface.
findings.evidence: Block-type census of frontend/public/reader/topic-chapters/carboxylic-acid-derivatives.json: Counter({'molecule': 35, 'text': 11, 'external_link': 11, 'video': 3, 'mcmurry_link': 1, 'reaction_coordinate': 1, 'image': 1}) — no practice block type. Every nugget in topic.package.json has a populated practice_check.
findings.recommended_outcome: Each reader section needs its authored self-check delivered inline with a reveal-able answer; if the reader cannot render one today that is a platform gap to raise rather than content to drop.

location.anchor_text: Name esters and amides by the IUPAC rules, including cyclic lactones and lactams.

findings.observation: The naming concept declares three objectives: name esters and amides including lactones and lactams; distinguish primary, secondary and tertiary amides by substitution at nitrogen; and recognize the five families. Only the third is directly assessed. Both short_answer items name esters (ethyl butanoate, isopropyl acetate) and nothing anywhere asks a student to name an amide, a lactone, a lactam, an acid chloride or an anhydride, or to classify an amide as primary/secondary/tertiary — the primary/tertiary distinction surfaces only implicitly, as an N-H band count in ch21-ir-identify-derivative-v2, which is tagged to the spectroscopy concept.
findings.learner_impact: Two of the section's three stated objectives carry no assessment, so a student can complete the chapter's naming practice without ever producing an amide or lactam name — despite the trouble_spots calling lactone/lactam recognition and the amide/amine confusion the section's main hazards.
findings.evidence: ch21-name-ester prompt 'Give the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH₂CO₂CH₂CH₃' and ch21-name-ester-v2 prompt 'Give the IUPAC name of CH₃CO₂CH(CH₃)₂' are the only short_answer items in the bank; concept acyl-derivative-structure-and-naming has six questions, four of which are the two categorize pairs and the two recognition items.
findings.recommended_outcome: The naming concept needs at least one item that requires producing an amide or lactam name and one that requires classifying amide substitution at nitrogen, so that all three of its stated objectives are assessed.

findings.observation: The chapter contains no worked example in the instructional sense — no problem stated, reasoned through step by step, and resolved. The eleven sections are expository prose with molecule figures; the closest thing is the acid-to-amide roadmap, which renders as an empty image (inst-002), and the practice_checks, which are not delivered (inst-011). Meanwhile the question bank asks students to do things that are never modelled: draw a tetrahedral intermediate with its formal charge, fill a bond-and-charge ledger for an elimination step, and assemble a two-step route.
findings.learner_impact: Students meet the graded tasks cold. The gap is widest for the two structure_scaffold items and the two bond_change_ledger items, where the chapter has described the reasoning in paragraphs but never shown it executed on a specific substrate.
findings.evidence: Reader block census shows 11 text blocks and 35 molecule blocks and no worked-example construct; ch21-tetrahedral-intermediate-draw (scaffold 'blank_canvas', answer CC([O-])(O)OC) and ch21-chloride-expulsion-ledger (four expected rows) have no modelled counterpart in any section.
findings.recommended_outcome: The mechanism section needs at least one fully worked substrate carried end to end — starting material, arrows, intermediate with charge, expulsion decision, product — so that the drawing and ledger tasks have a demonstrated procedure to imitate.

location.anchor_text: The attached heteroatom donates its lone pair strongly enough to give the bond substantial double-bond character

findings.observation: The matrix mixes absolute and comparative feature framings. The second row is explicitly comparative ('the weaker base of the two compared here') but the first is absolute, and its key marks methyl acetate 'Does not apply'. Esters do have appreciable π donation from the alkoxy oxygen — the C–O(R) bond is shortened, esters have a rotational barrier of roughly 10–14 kcal/mol, and the strong s-cis (Z) conformational preference of esters is the standard evidence for it. A student who knows that, and who reads the row as written, marks 'Applies' for the ester and is scored wrong.
findings.learner_impact: The better-prepared student is penalized for the more accurate answer, and the row teaches a false binary — that esters have no carbonyl–oxygen conjugation — that later chapters (ester enolate chemistry, conformational preferences) will have to reverse.
findings.evidence: ch21-ester-vs-amide-matrix.student_config.features[0].label (absolute) vs features[1].label ('the weaker base of the two compared here', comparative); answer_key [redacted].
findings.recommended_outcome: The donation row needs the same comparative framing as the leaving-group row, so the item asks which of the two compounds shows the effect more strongly rather than asserting that the ester does not show it.

location.anchor_text: https://openstax.org/books/organic-chemistry/pages/21-why-this-chapter

findings.observation: The chapter's only assigned-reading link is a single generic pointer to the OpenStax chapter-opener page ('21-why-this-chapter'), attached to section 1, with the boilerplate description 'Assigned reading in the OpenStax edition.' The house standard for a completed chapter is a set of specific OpenStax section links with a context sentence explaining why each is worth reading, and the chapter-opener URL is precisely the pattern that standard rules out. Every one of the eleven sections otherwise gets only a Wikipedia link, several of which are generic (Leaving_group for the reactivity ladder, Infrared_spectroscopy for the derivative-specific IR section).
findings.learner_impact: A student directed to read alongside this chapter lands on a chapter-opener page and has to find the relevant sections themselves; an instructor cannot point at a specific external section for saponification, amide reduction, or the IR correlation.
findings.evidence: frontend/public/reader/topic-chapters/carboxylic-acid-derivatives.json, section nugget-acyl-derivative-naming, block_type 'mcmurry_link', content.url = 'https://openstax.org/books/organic-chemistry/pages/21-why-this-chapter'; it is the only mcmurry_link block in the file (11 external_link blocks are all Wikipedia).
findings.recommended_outcome: The chapter needs its per-section OpenStax deep links with the one-sentence context each, matching the standard applied to the earlier chapters, and the two generic Wikipedia targets replaced with topic-specific ones.

location.anchor_text: Recognize an acid halide, an acid anhydride, an ester, an amide, and a nitrile as substituted acyl compounds.

findings.observation: The first learning objective names the nitrile as one of the families to be recognized, and the expanded text gives it a sentence. No asset, no figure, no question and no other section in the chapter involves a nitrile: none of the categorize items includes one, and nitrile hydrolysis, reduction and Grignard addition are absent. Nitriles are in fact developed fully in the preceding topic package (carboxylic-acids-and-nitriles, concepts nitrile-structure-naming-and-preparation and reactions-of-nitriles).
findings.learner_impact: A stated objective is never taught to a level that would let a student meet it and is never assessed, which inflates the chapter's apparent coverage and may lead an instructor to assume nitrile chemistry is assigned here.
findings.evidence: nugget-acyl-derivative-naming.learning_objectives[0]; the string 'nitrile' appears exactly once in the chapter body (text.expanded of nugget 1) and in no asset, question, or answer key; carboxylic-acids-and-nitriles/topic.package.json contains 258 occurrences and dedicated concepts.
findings.recommended_outcome: Either the objective's nitrile clause is removed and replaced by a pointer to the preceding chapter, or the recognition items include a nitrile so the objective is actually met.

location.anchor_text: NaCl, H₂O

findings.observation: The route builder offers the reagent 'NaCl, H₂O' alongside the candidate intermediate 'sodium benzoate'. Sodium chloride does not deprotonate benzoic acid — chloride is the conjugate base of a strong acid and the proton transfer is uphill by about twelve pKa units — so no reagent in the list actually produces the sodium benzoate node. The pairing is presented without comment, and the feedback addresses only the ladder direction.
findings.learner_impact: A student who selects that reagent/product pair receives no correction of the underlying acid–base error and may leave believing that a neutral salt can convert a carboxylic acid to its carboxylate.
findings.evidence: ch21-benzamide-synthesis-route.student_config.reagents[3] = {'id': 'r_nacl', 'text': 'NaCl, H₂O'}; intermediates[3] = {'id': 'm_salt', 'text': 'sodium benzoate', 'structure_smiles': '[O-]C(=O)c1ccccc1'}; feedback_bundle addresses only ladder direction and base for HCl.
findings.recommended_outcome: Either the distractor reagent should be one that genuinely gives the sodium benzoate node (a hydroxide or bicarbonate), or the feedback needs to name why a chloride salt cannot deprotonate a carboxylic acid.

location.anchor_text: A compound of formula C₄H₆O₃

findings.observation: The stated molecular formula C₄H₆O₃ is satisfied by exactly one of the four options: RDKit gives C4H6O3 for acetic anhydride, C3H6O2 for methyl acetate, C2H5NO for acetamide and C2H3ClO for acetyl chloride. The item can therefore be answered from the formula alone, and the infrared evidence — the two-band anhydride signature the section exists to teach — is never needed. The variant ch21-ir-identify-derivative-v2 is designed correctly for contrast: propanamide and N,N-dimethylformamide are both C₃H₇NO, so the N–H band count does the discriminating work.
findings.learner_impact: The base item does not measure IR interpretation, so the concept's surfaced pair contains one genuine spectroscopy item rather than two.
findings.evidence: ch21-ir-identify-derivative.prompt_text specifies C₄H₆O₃; RDKit formulas of options a–d: C4H6O3, C3H6O2, C2H5NO, C2H3ClO. ch21-ir-identify-derivative-v2 options a and b are both C3H7NO.
findings.recommended_outcome: The base item needs option candidates that share the stated formula, so that the pair of carbonyl bands rather than atom counting selects the answer.

location.anchor_text: which is how nylon 6 is made from caprolactam

findings.observation: Caprolactam is presented as an ordinary step-growth monomer 'carrying one of each functional group', within a section whose organizing contrast is step-growth versus chain-growth. Caprolactam carries no free amine and no free acid; it must first ring-open, and the industrial anionic route is a ring-opening chain-growth polymerization in which an activated chain end consumes monomer. Classifying it as step-growth is a simplification that sits directly next to the passage teaching students how to tell the two mechanisms apart.
findings.learner_impact: A student asked later to sort polymerizations by mechanism has been shown a chain-growth process filed under step-growth, in the very section that teaches the discrimination.
findings.evidence: nugget-step-growth-polymers text.standard: 'A single monomer that carries one of each functional group polymerizes equally well, which is how nylon 6 is made from caprolactam'; the same nugget contrasts step- and chain-growth in detail, and ch21-monomer-pairs-categorize asks students to apply that contrast.
findings.recommended_outcome: The polymer section needs caprolactam identified as a ring-opening case rather than folded into the step-growth definition, or an explicit note that the lactam must hydrolyse to the amino acid before the step-growth argument applies.

location.anchor_text: so the resulting iminium ion is reduced by a second hydride to give an amine

findings.observation: The hydride reduction of amides is described generically as passing through an iminium ion. That is right for tertiary amides (the practice_check correctly uses N,N-dimethylacetamide), but for primary and secondary amides the species formed after loss of the oxygen is a neutral imine, not an iminium ion — and the chapter's own drawing question uses a secondary amide, N-methylbenzamide.
findings.learner_impact: A student asked to write the intermediate for the graded case (ch21-amide-reduction-draw, N-methylbenzamide) will produce a charged species that cannot be drawn with a neutral nitrogen, and the formal-charge bookkeeping the chapter otherwise enforces breaks down.
findings.evidence: nugget-amide-reactions text.expanded: 'the tetrahedral intermediate then expels the oxygen, not the nitrogen, so the resulting iminium ion is reduced by a second hydride to give an amine'; ch21-amide-reduction-draw prompt uses N-methylbenzamide (answer_key.smiles CNCc1ccccc1, verified correct).
findings.recommended_outcome: The amide-reduction passage needs the intermediate described in a way that covers primary and secondary amides (imine) as well as tertiary (iminium), matching the substrates actually used in the questions.

location.anchor_text: hydrolyse

findings.observation: This chapter is written in British orthography ('hydrolyse'/'hydrolysed' 8×, 'favourable' 2×, 'colour' 3×, 'aluminium' 21×) while mixing in American '-ize' forms ('delocalized', 'neutralize', 'polymerization') and 'sulfur'. The adjacent chapters use American forms: the preceding aldehydes-and-ketones package has 'hydrolyze' 10× and the following carbonyl-alpha-substitution package has 'hydrolyze' 16×; 'aluminum' is used in acids-bases-and-curved-arrows and electrophilic-aromatic-substitution.
findings.learner_impact: A student reading consecutive chapters sees the same operation spelled hydrolyzed, hydrolysed, then hydrolyzed again, and the same reagent as lithium aluminum hydride then lithium aluminium hydride. It is cosmetic per chapter but reads as inconsistent editing across a course.

findings.recommended_outcome: The chapter's orthography needs to be brought into line with the corpus convention used by its neighbours, and made internally consistent rather than mixing -yse with -ize.

findings.observation: Because the bank surfaces one of each variant pair, two concepts are assessed by a single item each: reactions-of-acid-anhydrides (ch21-anhydride-acetylation, aspirin) and biological-acyl-transfer (ch21-thioester-vs-ester). For anhydrides, the objective 'Justify the industrial preference for acetic anhydride over acetyl chloride' is reachable only through one row of a matrix item tagged to a different concept, and the cyclic-anhydride behaviour is assessed only if the student happens to be served the variant. By contrast the mechanism and ester concepts get four surfaced items each.
findings.learner_impact: Two of the chapter's ten concepts carry a single point of assessment evidence, so an instructor cannot tell from the bank whether a student understands anhydride atom economy or biological acyl activation.
findings.evidence: Per-concept question counts in topic.package.json: reactions-of-acid-anhydrides 2 and biological-acyl-transfer 2 (one base plus one variant each) versus nucleophilic-acyl-substitution-mechanism 8 and reactions-of-esters 8; compiled counts {'surfaced': 24, 'staged_variants': 24}.
findings.recommended_outcome: The anhydride and biological-acyl-transfer concepts each need at least one further surfaced item so their stated objectives are covered independently of which variant a student is served.

findings.observation: The energy profile's minima are labelled 'Acetyl chloride + methoxide', 'Tetrahedral intermediate' and 'Methyl acetate + chloride', but minima_molecules draws only one species at each terminus — CC(=O)Cl at minimum 0 and COC(C)=O at minimum 2 — so the methoxide that is about to attack and the chloride that has just left are named in the label but absent from the drawn structure. The intermediate itself is drawn correctly (CC([O-])(Cl)OC, verified C3H6ClO2⁻).

findings.observation: Every asset carries both an alt_text and a substantially richer long_description (for example the tetrahedral intermediate's long_description names all four substituents and identifies which two could be expelled — the whole point of the figure), but only alt_text survives compilation. strengths: Chemical accuracy of the assets and answer keys is high. I canonicalized all 21 asset SMILES, the 3 synthesis-roadmap nodes and the 3 reaction-coordinate minima with RDKit; all parse, and every molecular formula matches the compound's stated identity (acetic anhydride C4H6O3, succinic anhydride C4H4O3, caprolactam C6H11NO as a seven-membered ring, sodium stearate C18H35NaO2 matching the alt text's eighteen carbons, acetyl phosphate C2H5O5P).

All 24 surfaced answer keys are correct. The acid-chloride reagent matrix is textbook-clean and mass-balanced (LiAlH4 → ethanol, Me2CuLi → acetone, excess MeMgBr → tert-butanol, EtOH/pyridine → ethyl acetate), the mixed anhydride from sodium acetate and benzoyl chloride is drawn correctly, both hydride-reduction keys distinguish the ester (alcohol) from the amide (amine) cases, and the saponification stoichiometry items (1 equiv for a monoester, 3 for a triacylglycerol) are right for the right reason.

The two reaction_coordinate_reasoning items are internally consistent with their own control points: the first profile's highest transition state is ts_1 at 8.0 so the key correctly says step 1, and the variant's is ts_2 at 25.0 so the key correctly says step 2 — the deliberate non-first rate-determining step in the variant is good pedagogy against the common 'the first barrier is always rate-determining' error.

Curved-arrow site ids map exactly onto the RDKit atom ordering of the multi-fragment SMILES in both mechanism items (methoxide oxygen at index 0 attacking the acyl carbon at index 3; ammonia nitrogen at index 0 attacking the acyl carbon at index 2), so the arrows land where the labels say they do.

The IR section is accurate and unusually well built: the correlation of carbonyl frequency with π donation, the anhydride two-band signature, the ester C–O stretch at 1150–1250 cm⁻¹, the primary/secondary/tertiary N–H band count, and the correct note that esters absorb above ketones because inductive withdrawal outweighs π donation. The identification variant is designed so the formula cannot short-circuit the spectroscopy (propanamide and DMF are both C₃H₇NO).

The chapter is genuinely mechanism-first rather than a reaction list: one mechanism is established, the reactivity ladder is derived from two named effects rather than asserted, and the ladder is then used to explain synthesis direction, biological activation, and the IR ordering. The error_repair, structured_reasoning and comparison_matrix items all reward that causal reasoning rather than recall.

Fifteen question types across ten concepts with an even core/standard/advanced spread, every item carrying a three-level hint ladder and a substantive generic_incorrect_explanation, and per-option wrong-answer explanations on the single_select and multi_select items that name the specific misconception rather than restating the key.

All eleven authored practice_check model answers are chemically correct, including the harder ones (N,N-dimethylethylamine from LiAlH4 on N,N-dimethylacetamide; the 50%-yield methylamine stoichiometry argument; acetic anhydride identified from C₄H₆O₃ plus a band pair).

The compiled question-set is byte-identical to the package for prompt_text, student_config, answer_key, feedback_bundle and accessibility_bundle across all 48 items — no compile-time drift, and the numeric items use the {mode, amount} tolerance shape rather than a bare number.
open_questions: I could not verify at the renderer level whether the curved_arrow workspace handles a multi-fragment molecule_smiles ('[O-]C.CC(=O)Cl' and 'N.ClC(=O)c1ccccc1'). The site ids are correct against RDKit atom order, but if the workspace lays out only the first fragment these two items become unanswerable. Worth a render check before seeding.

topic_tags and representation_tags are empty on all 48 compiled questions. This is corpus-wide rather than chapter-specific (only alkyl-halide-substitution-and-elimination, alkynes-organic-synthesis and organohalides have them populated), so I have not raised it as a finding, but it does mean this bank cannot be filtered by representation for assignment building.

The collapse to acetamide plus methoxide is correct and balanced, so I have not flagged it as an error, but an instructor may want it replaced by the neutral-amine pathway the chapter actually teaches.

The chapter never states where a carboxylic acid or a thioester sits on the reactivity ladder even though both are compared to it (inst-005, inst-009). If the intent is to keep the ladder to four rungs, the two comparison questions that reach outside it should say so explicitly.

Whether the empty roadmap image block (inst-002) and the dropped practice_check and long_description content (inst-011, inst-025) are chapter defects or known compiler/reader platform gaps affecting other chapters too — the fixes differ, and the orchestrator may already be tracking these as platform tickets.

personas.summary: The chapter is well organized around one mechanism and one reactivity ladder, and the question bank is genuinely broad (48 items, 15 types, every concept assessed), but for a student with weak prerequisites the reader itself gives almost nothing to hold on to. Eleven long prose sections arrive with no checkpoints, no worked examples, no summary and no ladder graphic; the eleven per-nugget practice checks that exist in the source package are never compiled into the reader, and the one synthesis roadmap compiles to an empty image block. Several places actively mislead me: the chapter states 'the weaker base is expelled' as the single principle governing every reaction, then has alkoxide (the stronger base) expelled in saponification with only a subordinate clause of justification; the IR section tells me frequency order equals reactivity order and then gives me an ester above a ketone; the acid-halide section says a ketone is 'more reactive' than the acid chloride it came from, one section after teaching me acid chlorides are the most reactive of all. The curved-arrow question lets me draw one arrow when the prose just told me the step takes two. Acid-catalysed substitution and amide-to-amine reduction are asserted in single sentences and then assessed by blank-canvas drawing questions. Nothing is strictly impossible to answer — the hint ladders are consistently three levels and usually rescue me — so I report no hard blocker, but I would stall, reread, and guess in at least six identifiable places.

location.anchor_text: The acyl group and the five families of carboxylic acid derivatives

findings.observation: The first section is titled 'the five families', and its first learning objective says 'Recognize an acid halide, an acid anhydride, an ester, an amide, and a nitrile as substituted acyl compounds.' A nitrile then appears exactly once, in a subordinate clause, and never again: there is no nitrile structure among the 23 assets, no nitrile concept, no nitrile reaction, no nitrile IR band, and none of the 48 questions mentions one. Meanwhile the reactivity, matrix and IR questions all say 'the four principal derivative families' and the classify-derivatives questions offer four groups.
findings.learner_impact: I count four families in every figure, every ladder and every question, but the heading and the objective promise five. I assume I have missed a whole section, scroll back through the chapter looking for it, and end up unsure whether nitriles are examinable. If they are, I have nothing to study from: I have never been shown a C≡N drawn, or told how to name one.
findings.evidence: nugget-acyl-derivative-naming title and learning_objectives[0]; the only nitrile sentence is 'A nitrile is included with these families by convention because hydrolysis converts it to the same carboxylic acid, although its carbon is sp-hybridized rather than sp².' Compare ch21-carbonyl-ir-wavenumber prompt: 'the four principal derivative families'.
findings.recommended_outcome: The chapter needs to either teach and assess the nitrile family at the same minimum level as the other four (a structure I can see, a name I can form, and at least one question), or stop promising it in the title and the objective and count consistently as four throughout.

location.anchor_text: which is the more basic of the two available leaving groups but is nevertheless lost

findings.observation: Section 2 gives me one universal rule: 'When the tetrahedral intermediate carries two potential leaving groups, the weaker base is expelled. That single principle sets both the direction of every interconversion in this chapter and the reactivity order of the derivatives.' Section 6 then breaks that rule on the chapter's most important reaction and repairs it in half a sentence: alkoxide is expelled even though it 'is the more basic of the two available leaving groups', 'because the alternative is expelling hydroxide and returning to starting material.' The generalization a student actually needs — that when the two candidate groups are of comparable basicity the product-determining outcome is set by a downstream irreversible step, not by the elimination step alone — is never stated.
findings.learner_impact: I apply the rule I was told is universal, predict that hydroxide leaves again and nothing happens, and conclude either that esters do not saponify or that I have misunderstood basicity. Because the exception is buried mid-paragraph, I read it as a typo and keep the wrong rule. On ch21-saponification-products I then guess on option (d) about whether hydroxide is consumed.
findings.evidence: nugget-addition-elimination text.standard; nugget-ester-hydrolysis text.standard and text.expanded ('this last step is strongly exergonic and effectively irreversible'); ch21-saponification-products options a/c/d and ch21-grignard-ester-error-v2 both test the consumed-equivalent consequence.
findings.recommended_outcome: The chapter needs the leaving-group rule stated with its scope and its exception together at the point it is introduced, so a learner knows in advance that saponification is decided by the proton transfer that follows and not by comparing the two groups on the tetrahedral carbon.

location.anchor_text: The steps are the same; only the charges differ.

findings.observation: The acid-catalysed pathway is disposed of in three sentences ('Protonation of the carbonyl oxygen raises the electrophilicity... The steps are the same; only the charges differ') and in one compressed chain in the ester nugget ('proton transfers within the tetrahedral intermediate convert the alkoxy group into an alcohol, which then departs as a neutral molecule'). No figure shows a protonated carbonyl, a neutral tetrahedral intermediate, or the internal proton transfer; the chapter's only mechanism figure and only energy profile are both for the anionic methoxide-plus-acetyl-chloride case.
findings.learner_impact: The step I always get stuck on is exactly the one that is skipped — which oxygen gets protonated, when, and how the alkoxy group turns into an alcohol. Three questions put me in acidic conditions (ch21-amide-reduction-draw-v2, ch21-ester-reduction-product-v2, and the acid-hydrolysis half of ch21-amide-hydrolysis-conditions) and I answer them by remembering product names rather than by tracing anything, which is exactly the habit that fails me on an exam.
findings.evidence: nugget-addition-elimination text.expanded final paragraph; nugget-ester-hydrolysis text.expanded paragraph 3; assets list contains no protonated species (mol-tetrahedral-intermediate is the anionic CC([O-])(Cl)OC only).
findings.recommended_outcome: The chapter needs one fully worked acid-catalysed substitution — every intermediate shown as a drawn species with its charges — because three questions require reasoning through charges the prose only asserts are 'the same'.

location.anchor_text: Draw the single curved arrow for the first step of the mechanism.

findings.observation: The prose teaches that the addition step takes two curved arrows: 'Two curved arrows record this step: one runs from the lone pair of the nucleophile to the carbonyl carbon, and a second runs from the carbon–oxygen π bond to the oxygen.' The question asks for 'the single curved arrow for the first step' and sets max_arrows: 1, accepting only the nucleophile-to-carbon arrow. Its level-3 hint even describes the second arrow I am forbidden to draw: 'The carbonyl carbon accepts the electron pair, and the π electrons move onto oxygen as it does.' The same conflict is in ch21-addition-elimination-arrow-v2.
findings.learner_impact: I draw the arrow I was taught, try to add the second one, and the workspace refuses. I do not conclude the question is simplified — I conclude my two-arrow reading of the mechanism was wrong, delete my correct arrow, and start guessing. On any exam that asks for 'the mechanism', I now under-draw.
findings.evidence: nugget-addition-elimination text.expanded paragraph 1; ch21-addition-elimination-arrow student_config.max_arrows = 1, answer_key.expected_arrows has one entry; feedback_bundle.hints[2].
findings.recommended_outcome: The arrow question and the prose need to agree on how many arrows the addition step takes, or the prompt needs to say explicitly which of the two arrows it is asking for and that the other one is still part of the step.

location.anchor_text: a ketone is more electrophilic than the acid chloride's substitution product would suggest

findings.observation: The sentence explaining double Grignard addition is circular and contradicts the ladder taught one section earlier. The ketone IS the acid chloride's substitution product, so 'a ketone is more electrophilic than the acid chloride's substitution product would suggest' compares the species to itself; and the shorter version says the reagent adds 'to that more reactive ketone', which directly contradicts 'acid halide > anhydride > ester > amide' with the acid chloride at the top. The correct account — that a ketone is more electrophilic than an ester or amide because it has no donating heteroatom, and that the ladder covers only heteroatom-substituted acyl compounds — appears only in the ester section ('that new carbonyl compound is more electrophilic than the ester was, because it lacks the electron-donating alkoxy group') and is never connected back.
findings.learner_impact: I have just memorized that the acid chloride is the most reactive thing in the chapter, so 'the more reactive ketone' reads as a contradiction and I stop trusting the ladder. I cannot answer 'why does it not just stop?' for myself, so on ch21-acid-chloride-products-v2 I match reagents to products by counting carbons and hoping, and I have no rule for when a carbonyl compound gets attacked twice.
findings.evidence: nugget-acid-halide-reactions text.expanded paragraph 3 and text.standard; contrast nugget-reactivity-ladder text.standard ('acid halide > anhydride > ester > amide') and nugget-ester-other-reactions text.expanded paragraph 4; assessed by ch21-acid-chloride-products-v2 and ch21-grignard-equivalents.
findings.recommended_outcome: The chapter needs one clear statement of where ketones and aldehydes sit relative to the four derivative families, given once and used in both the acid-halide and ester sections, so 'it adds twice' has a reason a learner can reconstruct rather than a self-referential sentence.

location.anchor_text: lithium tri-tert-butoxyaluminium hydride at −78 °C is attenuated enough to deliver the aldehyde

findings.observation: One 7-minute section introduces thionyl chloride plus its chlorosulfite intermediate, oxalyl chloride, four heteroatom nucleophiles with their four products, the base requirement and the ammonium-salt failure mode, Grignard double addition, lithium diorganocopper reagents and how they are prepared, lithium aluminium hydride, and lithium tri-tert-butoxyaluminium hydride at −78 °C — roughly ten reagents and eight products in three paragraphs. The reader delivers this with two molecule figures (benzoyl chloride, acetyl chloride), an empty image block, and no table, no product structures, and no checkpoint.
findings.learner_impact: This is where I stop reading and start highlighting. There is no product structure to anchor any of the eight transformations, so I try to memorize reagent-name-to-product-name pairs, mix up the two attenuated hydride reagents (which one goes with the acid chloride and which with the ester?), and go into ch21-acid-chloride-products-v2 — marked 'advanced' — with nothing but name recall.
findings.evidence: nugget-acid-halide-reactions text.expanded (three paragraphs, duration_minutes 7); reader section nugget-acid-halide-reactions contains blocks blk-z4s7hany, blk-p6ds8eti (two molecules), blk-w6qmft0f (empty image), blk-ozox8sn3 (Wikipedia link) and nothing else. The reader's default detail level is 'expanded', the densest of the three written versions.
findings.recommended_outcome: This section needs its reagent load either split or made scannable — a learner should be able to see each transformation's product, and to tell the two partial-reduction reagents apart, without holding ten reagent names in working memory at once.

location.anchor_text: Name CH₃CH₂CO₂CH₃ and state which fragment comes from the alcohol.

findings.observation: All eleven nuggets carry a practice_check with a prompt and a model answer, and none of them reaches the reader: a search of the compiled chapter for 'practice' and for any practice-check text returns zero hits, and the compiled block types are only text, molecule, reaction_coordinate, image, video, external_link and mcmurry_link. There is no callout, no summary, no self-check and no worked example anywhere in the 11-section chapter, and the only external reading pointer is a single chapter-level OpenStax link to '21-why-this-chapter'.
findings.learner_impact: I read eleven long expanded prose sections end to end with no place to stop and test whether any of it stuck, and no worked problem modelling how an answer is supposed to be written. I believe I understand it because I have read it, then discover in the question bank that I cannot do it. When I stall on saponification there is no targeted place to go — the one further-reading link is the chapter's opening page.
findings.evidence: topic.package.json nuggets[*].practice_check (11 present, e.g. nugget-acyl-derivative-naming, nugget-addition-elimination, nugget-ester-hydrolysis); grep of frontend/public/reader/topic-chapters/carboxylic-acid-derivatives.json for those prompts returns 0; block_type counts: 11 text, 35 molecule, 11 external_link, 1 mcmurry_link, 1 image, 3 video, 1 reaction_coordinate.
findings.recommended_outcome: The eleven checkpoints that were already authored need to reach the page a student reads, and at least the mechanism and stoichiometry sections need a worked answer a learner can imitate — reading-only delivery leaves a low-confidence student with no way to detect that they have not learned it.

location.anchor_text: Benzoic acid to N-methylbenzamide by way of the acid chloride

findings.observation: The synthesis roadmap compiles into reader block blk-w6qmft0f as an image with url: "" and is not hidden (unlike the three video blocks, which are is_hidden: true). The block still carries a caption and an alt text describing a three-structure, two-arrow scheme with reagents and a highlighted target that no student will ever see.
findings.learner_impact: I get a blank frame with a caption promising exactly the figure I need — the one picture in the chapter that shows the direction of travel up and back down the ladder. I assume it failed to load, reload the page, and eventually move on believing I have missed something. The reasoning it was meant to carry is then required by ch21-benzamide-synthesis-route and ch21-benzamide-synthesis-route-v2.
findings.evidence: frontend/public/reader/topic-chapters/carboxylic-acid-derivatives.json block blk-w6qmft0f: {block_type: 'image', content.url: '', alt_text: 'A two-step forward synthesis: benzoic acid is treated with thionyl chloride...'}; source asset roadmap-acid-to-amide has a full node/step spec.

location.anchor_text: chloride, a carboxylate, an alkoxide, and an amide anion form a series of increasing basicity

findings.observation: The chapter's central argument rests on comparing leaving-group basicity, but it never gives me the numbers to compare with. Basicity is described only in words ('the conjugate base of a strong acid', 'a strong base', 'stronger still'), and the only pKa values in any nugget are 5 and 16 in the ester-hydrolysis section. The actual reference values appear once — inside a distractor-bearing option of ch21-why-amide-least-reactive ('pKa near −7... pKa near 38') — and questions and hints elsewhere ask me to compare a thiol with an alcohol (ch21-thioester-vs-ester hint 2) and a carboxylic acid with an alcohol (ch21-why-amide-least-reactive-v2) using values I was never given.
findings.learner_impact: Every ranking task reduces to recalling the sentence order in which the four families were listed, which is exactly the memorization the chapter's own trouble_spots warn against. When ch21-reactivity-rank-v2 inserts a thioester into the list, my memorized sentence has no slot for it and I guess. I cannot check my own ranking against anything.
findings.evidence: nugget-reactivity-ladder text.standard and text.expanded contain no pKa values; nugget-ester-hydrolysis is the only place pKa appears (5, 16, 'eleven pKa units'); ch21-why-amide-least-reactive evidence option 'pka'; ch21-thioester-vs-ester hints[1] 'Compare the pKa of a thiol with that of an alcohol.'
findings.recommended_outcome: The learner needs the leaving-group basicity comparison available as data in the reading — one place that pairs each departing group with its conjugate-acid pKa — because four question types ask them to reason from basicities the chapter only characterizes with adjectives.

location.anchor_text: The order of the frequencies is the same as the order of reactivity

findings.observation: The spectroscopy section gives me a rule — 'The order of the frequencies is the same as the order of reactivity, which follows because both are governed by the same donation' — and, three sentences later, the data that breaks it: esters absorb 'near 1735 cm⁻¹ — slightly higher than the roughly 1715 cm⁻¹ of a ketone, since the inductive withdrawal by the ester oxygen outweighs its π donation.' Induction is introduced here and nowhere else; the reactivity section explains everything by π donation alone. The ketone value is then used as an anchor in the hints of both ch21-carbonyl-ir-wavenumber and its v2.
findings.learner_impact: I apply the rule I was just handed to the two numbers I was just handed and conclude that an ester is more reactive than a ketone — a wrong belief that survives into the aldehyde/ketone material and makes the 'the ketone is attacked immediately' claim in the ester section look impossible. Nothing in the chapter contradicts me, so I never find out.
findings.evidence: nugget-spectroscopy-acyl-derivatives text.standard ('The order of the frequencies is the same as the order of reactivity') and text.expanded (ester 1735 vs ketone 1715 with the inductive-withdrawal caveat); ch21-carbonyl-ir-wavenumber hints[0] 'Start from the ester value of about 1735 cm⁻¹'; ch21-carbonyl-ir-wavenumber-v2 hints[0] 'Start from the ketone value of about 1715 cm⁻¹'.
findings.recommended_outcome: The frequency-tracks-reactivity rule needs to be stated with the ketone counterexample attached, so the one pair of numbers the chapter hands the learner cannot be used to derive the opposite of what the chapter teaches.

location.anchor_text: rate_determining_step

findings.observation: Both reaction-coordinate questions ask for step_count, rate_determining_step, overall and step_types, with expected answers 'endergonic'/'exergonic' and a rate-determining step that is step 1 in the parent and step 2 in the variant. The strings 'rate-determining' and 'endergonic' appear zero times across all thirty-three nugget texts; 'exergonic' appears once, in passing, about a proton transfer. The rc-addition-elimination figure in the reader is labelled only with minima names and never marks or names a transition state, and its accessible long description likewise never uses either term.
findings.learner_impact: I am asked to name the rate-determining step of a mechanism whose chapter never uses the phrase and never points at a transition state on the one profile I was shown. I fall back on 'the first step is always the slow one', which is right by luck in the parent question and wrong in the variant, so my score tells me nothing about what I actually misunderstand. The hints rescue the mechanics but only after I have already guessed.
findings.evidence: ch21-addition-elimination-profile and -v2 student_config.ask; answer_key.expected.step_types ['endergonic','exergonic'], rate_determining_step 1 vs 2; word counts over topic.package.json nuggets: 'rate-determining' 0, 'endergonic' 0, 'exergonic' 1; asset rc-addition-elimination accessibility.long_description names no transition state.
findings.recommended_outcome: Either the reading needs to name and locate a transition state and define rate-determining and endergonic where the profile is first shown, or these questions need to stop assuming vocabulary this chapter never uses.

location.anchor_text: so the resulting iminium ion is reduced by a second hydride to give an amine

findings.observation: Amide reduction is the one reaction in the chapter that breaks the pattern, and it is delivered in two asserted sentences. The shorter version gives no reason at all ('because the intermediate collapses by expelling oxygen rather than nitrogen'); the longer one introduces an iminium ion that is never defined, never drawn, and never mentioned again. No figure shows the intermediate, the iminium, or the second hydride delivery, and the chapter never reconciles 'the oxygen is expelled' with the leaving-group rule from section 2.
findings.learner_impact: I am then asked to draw the product on a blank canvas (ch21-amide-reduction-draw) with no picture of any step to imitate. I memorize 'amide gives amine' as an exception with no mechanism attached, which means I cannot handle it when the substrate is anything but the two I was shown, and 'iminium ion' becomes a word I skip over.
findings.evidence: nugget-amide-reactions text.standard and text.expanded paragraph 3; asset list for this nugget contains only mol-acetamide, mol-n-methylacetamide, mol-benzamide (no intermediate); ch21-amide-reduction-draw student_config.scaffold = 'blank_canvas' with only text hints.
findings.recommended_outcome: The amide-to-amine divergence needs a visible intermediate sequence and a stated reason for expelling oxygen rather than nitrogen, since it is assessed by a from-scratch drawing task and is the one place the chapter's general rule appears to be overridden.

location.anchor_text: the ladder can be used directly for synthesis planning

findings.observation: The word 'ladder' carries the whole chapter — it appears eight times across the nuggets, in phrases like 'down the ladder', 'up the ladder', 'the top of the reactivity ladder' and 'sit just below acid halides on the reactivity ladder' — and it is never drawn. The reader represents it as four separate molecule cards stacked one after another (acetyl chloride, acetic anhydride, methyl acetate, acetamide) with no ordering, no arrow and no direction marker. The one asset that would have shown it, video-reactivity-ladder, compiles to a hidden block with an empty url.
findings.learner_impact: 'Down the ladder' is a spatial instruction and I have no picture to move down. I have to re-derive which direction is which every time, and on ch21-benzamide-synthesis-route the whole task is choosing a direction. Four identical-looking molecule cards in a row do not tell me they are a sequence.
findings.evidence: nugget-reactivity-ladder text.expanded ('Reactions proceed down the ladder', 'Moving up the ladder requires hydrolysis back to the carboxylic acid'); reader blocks blk-rrajuygo, blk-l1b0vq29, blk-n80dn9nl, blk-vxjudis9 are four ungrouped molecule cards; blk-1ndwval0 is video with url '' and is_hidden true.
findings.recommended_outcome: The chapter's organizing metaphor needs to exist as something a learner can see ordered and directional, because prose alone cannot make 'down' mean anything and four ungrouped structure cards do not read as a ranking.

location.anchor_text: Two effects decide the order and both point the same way.

findings.observation: Only the twenty option-based questions (single_select and multi_select) carry per-answer explanations; the other twenty-eight — every ranking, matching, categorizing, matrix, ledger, drawing, numeric, short-answer, synthesis-route and error-repair item — have a single generic_incorrect_explanation that is identical no matter what the learner did. A student who swaps only ester and amide in ch21-reactivity-rank sees the same paragraph as a student who reverses the whole list; a student who misfiles only the anhydride in ch21-classify-derivatives is told to 'read each formula from the acyl carbon outward'.
findings.learner_impact: When I get one card out of four wrong, the feedback restates the method I already tried and never tells me which card was misplaced or why. I cannot tell a small slip from a broken concept, so I re-attempt by shuffling rather than by re-reasoning, and I learn nothing from being wrong.
findings.evidence: Compiled question-set: 28 of 48 questions have wrong_answer_explanations length 0 (e.g. ch21-reactivity-rank, ch21-classify-derivatives, ch21-acid-chloride-products, ch21-ester-vs-amide-matrix, ch21-chloride-expulsion-ledger, ch21-polyamide-monomers); the 20 option-based items have 2–3 each.
findings.recommended_outcome: The non-option question types need feedback that responds to the specific mistake — at minimum for the ranking and categorizing items, where the common error patterns are already named in the concepts' trouble_spots and could be addressed directly.

location.anchor_text: Nothing new is required to explain polymer formation from the chemistry already developed in this chapter

findings.observation: The polymer section opens by promising there is nothing new — 'the only change is that each monomer carries two reactive groups instead of one' — and then introduces a set of genuinely new ideas that are not acyl chemistry at all: the absence of an initiator, dimers combining with dimers, monomer disappearing early, high molecular weight arriving only at very high conversion, and a contrast with chain-growth polymerization including radical initiators. Four of the six items in ch21-monomer-pairs-categorize test exactly these new kinetics ideas.
findings.learner_impact: The opening tells me I can read this section quickly, so I do, and then a question asks me to sort 'High molecular weight is reached only at very high conversion' and 'Full-length chains coexist with unreacted monomer throughout' into two mechanisms I skimmed in one paragraph. False reassurance is worse than a warning: I do not go back, I guess.
findings.evidence: nugget-step-growth-polymers text.expanded paragraphs 1 and 3; ch21-monomer-pairs-categorize items i1–i4 and i6, all drawn from that single kinetics paragraph.
findings.recommended_outcome: The step-versus-chain-growth kinetics contrast needs to be flagged as new material and given the same weight in the reading as it has in the assessment, rather than being introduced under a reassurance that nothing new is coming.

location.anchor_text: A backside displacement is geometrically impossible here

findings.observation: The reason acyl substitution is not an SN2 is asserted rather than shown: 'A backside displacement is geometrically impossible here: the carbonyl carbon is sp²-hybridized and planar.' Planarity alone does not obviously forbid attack opposite the leaving group, and no figure contrasts the two geometries. The curved-arrow question's generic feedback then repeats the same unexplained assertion back at me ('An arrow drawn to the chlorine or to a carbon–chlorine bond describes a one-step substitution, which cannot occur at a planar sp² carbon'). The neighbouring sentence 'no bond is ever broken and formed at the same time as it is in an SN2 reaction' is also ambiguous on a first read.
findings.learner_impact: This is the single question I would most want answered — why does the mechanism I spent a whole chapter learning not apply here? — and I get the same sentence twice, once in the reading and once as the explanation of why my answer was wrong. Feedback that restates the claim I did not understand does not help me; I accept it as a rule to memorize and stop asking.
findings.evidence: nugget-addition-elimination text.standard and text.expanded paragraph 1; ch21-addition-elimination-arrow feedback_bundle.generic_incorrect_explanation; no asset contrasts sp³ backside attack with acyl addition.
findings.recommended_outcome: The learner needs the SN2-versus-addition contrast made visible or argued rather than asserted, and the wrong-answer feedback needs to teach something the reading did not already say in the same words.

location.anchor_text: Methyl carbon attached to the central carbon

findings.observation: The ledger questions ask me to type bond entries like '1-3' against a numbered atom legend, but the reference structure rendered beside the legend is a plain RDKit drawing with no atom numbers on it (the renderer produces the SVG with no atomNote labels). The legend is also imprecise: the molecule CC([O-])(Cl)OC contains two methyl carbons, and label '5: Methyl carbon attached to the central carbon' names one of them while the other methyl — the one on the methoxy oxygen — is left unlabelled, even though a methoxy oxygen label ('4') is provided.
findings.learner_impact: I am asked to record changes by atom number while looking at a picture with no numbers on it, so I have to hold the five verbal descriptions in my head and hope I matched them to the right atoms. With two methyls in view and only one named, I second-guess whether '5' means the one I think it does, and on an 'advanced' question with a spurious-row penalty I add fewer rows than I should rather than risk being wrong.
findings.evidence: ch21-chloride-expulsion-ledger student_config.atom_labels and molecule_smiles 'CC([O-])(Cl)OC'; same pattern in -v2 with 'CC([O-])(N)OC'; [internal source reference — not in this repo] renders config.molecule.svgDataUri as a plain image plus a text legend, and molecule_visuals.render_molecule_visual draws the SVG without atom numbering.
findings.recommended_outcome: The ledger's numbered legend needs a structure a learner can actually map numbers onto, and every atom a learner might want to name should be named — otherwise the numbering is a memory task layered on top of the chemistry task.

location.anchor_text: coalesce only on warming

findings.observation: The restricted-rotation evidence is delivered through an NMR observation whose vocabulary is never explained: DMF's two methyls 'give separate NMR signals at room temperature and coalesce only on warming'. 'Coalesce' is not defined, and the idea of an NMR timescale appears only inside a level-3 hint of the question that tests it ('coalescence occurs when that rate becomes fast on the NMR timescale'). The variant question is graded 'advanced' and is one of only four questions on the amide concept.
findings.learner_impact: I can see that something changes on warming but not why an NMR spectrum should care about a rotation rate, so I answer ch21-amide-hydrolysis-conditions-v2 by elimination on the other three options rather than by understanding, and the 20 kcal/mol barrier stays a number I have read rather than evidence I can use.
findings.evidence: nugget-amide-reactions text.expanded paragraph 1; nugget-spectroscopy-acyl-derivatives text.expanded; ch21-amide-hydrolysis-conditions-v2 option a and hints[2].
findings.recommended_outcome: If the chapter uses a spectroscopic observation as its evidence for restricted rotation, the learner needs a bridge for what coalescence means and why a spectrum reports on a rate, since that reasoning is what the advanced question grades.

location.anchor_text: both are named with a Greek letter or a ring size that states how many atoms separate the carbonyl carbon from the heteroatom

findings.observation: Lactone and lactam naming is described only in that one clause, and the Greek-letter convention is never worked: γ-butyrolactone appears as a figure title with no statement of what γ counts from or to. Caprolactam and nylon 6 are likewise named without their numbering being explained.
findings.learner_impact: I can recognize the ring as an ester but I could not name one, and I cannot tell whether γ means the third carbon from the carbonyl or the fifth atom of the ring. Since both cyclic questions (ch21-recognize-lactone and its variant) ask me only to classify, I never find out that I cannot name them until an exam does.
findings.evidence: nugget-acyl-derivative-naming text.standard; asset mol-butyrolactone title 'γ-Butyrolactone, a cyclic ester' and its long_description, which explains the ring but not the letter; ch21-recognize-lactone tests classification only.
findings.recommended_outcome: Either the Greek-letter lactone convention needs one worked instance so a learner can apply it, or the naming objective should stop implying it is covered.

strengths: Every one of the ten concepts is assessed, with 24 surfaced questions plus 24 variants across 15 question types — no concept is left with only a drawing task or only a recall task.

The concepts' trouble_spots are real student errors, not generic warnings, and many of them are converted directly into distractors and wrong-answer explanations (the 'both acyl groups transfer' anhydride error, the 'two separate molecules' cyclic-anhydride error, the 'hydroxide is catalytic' saponification error).

The wrong-answer explanations on the twenty option-based questions are specific and diagnostic rather than scolding — ch21-ester-reduction-product option b names DIBAL-H at −78 °C as the fix, and ch21-amide-hydrolysis-conditions option d corrects 'inert' to 'slow' and points at proteases.
The paired energy-profile questions deliberately put the rate-determining step in step 1 in one and step 2 in the other, which is exactly the discrimination a memorizer would fail.

The tetrahedral-intermediate figure (mol-tetrahedral-intermediate) shows the charge explicitly and is the single most useful anchor in the chapter; the reader places it right beside the prose that needs it.

All 48 questions carry a three-level hint ladder that moves from a general orienting question to the specific fact, and level 1 hints reliably ask rather than tell — this is what keeps several under-explained sections answerable at all.
The pKa values a learner needs for the amide argument, though missing from the reading, are at least supplied inside ch21-why-amide-least-reactive's evidence options rather than assumed silently.
open_questions: Are the eleven authored practice_check items intended to reach the reader at all, or is their absence a compiler-level gap that affects every topic package? If it is platform-wide, this chapter still needs interim checkpoints in its prose.

Is the empty image block for roadmap-acid-to-amide (blk-w6qmft0f, url: "") a compile defect, or is the synthesis_roadmap spec expected to render client-side from the block's spec the way reaction_coordinate does?

The reader's default detail level is 'expanded' (useReaderPersonalization prefs), so the densest of the three authored variants is what a struggling reader sees first, including jargon such as 'the carbonyl π* orbital' that appears in no other variant. Is 'expanded' the intended default for this audience?
The chapter's only further-reading pointer is the chapter-level OpenStax '21-why-this-chapter' link; deeper section links exist for other chapters. Is that intentional for this package?
I coined no new categories; ss-017 was filed under figure-purpose because the defect is that the reference figure cannot serve the numbering task it is paired with, not that it is drawn incorrectly.

executive_summary: Baseline verdict is blocked, driven by two chapter-local blockers and three platform access blockers. The instructor persona independently re-parsed all 21 asset SMILES and all 48 answer keys in RDKit and found the chemistry otherwise sound — every formula matches its stated identity, both energy-profile keys read correctly off their own control points, and the curved-arrow site indices map exactly onto the SMILES atom order. The two chapter-local blockers were a genuinely wrong causal claim (a Grignard adds twice because the ketone is 'more reactive' than the acid chloride, which inverts the chapter's own reactivity ladder and is additionally circular, since the ketone IS the acid chloride's substitution product) and two recognition items whose four options each drew a different compound, so the key was the only option whose picture matched the stem. Both are corrected. A third defect was reported independently by all four personas: the chapter's only multi-step figure, the acid-to-amide synthesis roadmap, compiled to a visible image block with an empty URL — a caption and alt text promising a figure that renders as nothing. It has been replaced with a three-species molecule sequence and its reagent rationale moved into prose. The remaining blockers are platform-wide and identical in every already-published chapter of this series.
consensus_strengths: All 21 asset SMILES and all 48 answer keys verified correct in RDKit; every mass balance checked is exact.
No option set uses positional 'Structure A/B/C/D' labels, and every illustrated option set is uniformly illustrated — no lone-illustrated-option answer tell anywhere in the bank.
Every question type used is keyboard-complete through labelled Selects and IconButtons; no activity is drag-only, hover-only, or motion-dependent.
bond_change_ledger items are fully answerable without seeing the structure — atom_labels are self-describing text rendered as a list.
The paired energy-profile questions deliberately put the rate-determining step in step 1 in one and step 2 in the other, which a memoriser fails.
All 48 questions carry a three-level hint ladder whose level-1 hints ask rather than tell.

ranked_recommendations.title: Correct the double-Grignard explanation
ranked_recommendations.need: The stated reason for the second addition inverts the chapter's own reactivity ladder and is circular.
ranked_recommendations.rationale: The claim is factually wrong, not merely unclear; the least-complex fix is a prose correction in both the standard and expanded tiers that keeps the ladder intact and gives a real reason (a Grignard is nucleophilic enough to consume the ketone as fast as it forms, and ketones are not members of the heteroatom-substituted series the ladder ranks).

ranked_recommendations.title: Fix the two cyclic-derivative recognition items
ranked_recommendations.need: Each option drew a different compound, so the key was selectable by matching the picture to the stem without evaluating any claim.
ranked_recommendations.rationale: Showing the same subject structure on every option removes the tell while preserving the item's intent; no new asset is needed.

ranked_recommendations.title: Deliver the acid-to-amide sequence as figures that render
ranked_recommendations.need: The chapter's only multi-step figure compiled to a visible empty-URL image block.
ranked_recommendations.rationale: All four personas reported this independently. Rather than wait on the roadmap renderer, the three species are now molecule assets (which do render) and the roadmap's reagent rationale and caveats moved into the section prose — the same substitution ch23 used successfully.

ranked_recommendations.need: The chapter states 'the weaker base is expelled' as universal, then breaks it on its most important reaction with a half-sentence.
